(p-368) In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful

Surah al-Ahzab (The Confederates)

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿O Prophet﴾.

There is no contradiction between this and His saying at the end of the verse: ﴿Indeed, Allah is ever Acquainted with what you do﴾ [al-Ahzab: 2], in the plural form, because the Ummah enters under the specific address to the Prophet (ﷺ), since he is their exemplar, as its explanation has already been fully given in Surah "al-Rum".

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 33, verse 4 (part 1 of 7):

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Nor has He made your wives whom you divorce by zihar your mothers﴾.

In this word there are four Seven Readings (qira'at sab'iyyah). ʿĀṣim alone read: tuẓāhirūna, with a dammah on the tā', a light ẓā' after it, then an alif, then a kasrah on the hā' (lightened). Ḥamzah and al-Kisāʾī read: (taẓāharūna), with a fatḥah on the tā', followed by a fatḥah on the ẓā' (lightened), then an alif, then a fatḥah on the hā' (lightened). Ibn ʿĀmir alone read as the reading of Ḥamzah and al-Kisāʾī, except that Ibn ʿĀmir doubles the ẓā', whereas they lighten it. Nāfiʿ, Ibn Kathīr and Abū ʿAmr read: (taẓẓahharūna), with a fatḥah on the tā', followed by fatḥah-marked ẓā' and hā', both doubled, without an alif.

So His saying tuẓāhirūna, according to the reading of ʿĀṣim, is the imperfect of ẓāhara on the pattern fāʿala. According to the reading of Ḥamzah and al-Kisāʾī, it is the imperfect of taẓāhara on the pattern tafāʿala, in which one of the two tā's has been elided, according to the rule of his saying in the Khulāṣah (a didactic poem on grammar):

"And what begins with two tā's may be reduced to one tā, as in tabayyana (it became clear) — the lesson is clear."

So the original form, according to the reading of the two brothers, is tatazāharūna, and one of the two tā's was elided. According to the reading of Ibn ʿĀmir, it is also the imperfect of taẓāhara, like the reading of Ḥamzah and al-Kisāʾī, except that one of the two tā's was assimilated into the ẓā' and not elided; its perfect is iẓẓāhara, like iddāraka (Q. 27:66), ithāqaltum (Q. 9:38) and iddārawtum (Q. 2:72), meaning tadāraka (to overtake/catch up). Etc.

(p-189) According to the reading of Nāfiʿ, Ibn Kathīr and Abū ʿAmr, it is the imperfect of tazahhara on the pattern tafaʿʿala, its original form being tatazahharūna with two tā's, and one of the two tā's was assimilated into the ẓā'. Its perfect is iẓẓahhar, like iṭṭayyarnā (Q. 27:47) and izzayyanat (Q. 10:24), meaning taṭayyarnā (we took omen) and tazayyanat (she adorned herself), as we have already explained in Sūrat Ṭā-Hā, in the discussion of His saying: ﴿Then behold, it swallowed up what they had falsely fabricated﴾ (Q. 7:117).

From what we have mentioned it is known that their saying ẓāhara min imra'atihi, tazāhara minhā and tazahhara minhā all have one meaning, namely that he says to her: "You are to me like the back of my mother," meaning that she is forbidden to him. In the pre-Islamic period they used to divorce with this formula.

Allah, may He be exalted, has made clear in His saying here: ﴿Nor has He made your wives whom you divorce by zihar your mothers﴾ that whoever says to his wife, "You are to me like the back of my mother," she does not become his mother by that. He did not add anything here to this, but He, may He be exalted, clarified this in Sūrat al-Mujādilah, explaining that the wives of those who make zihar from them are not their mothers, that their mothers are only the women who bore them specifically and no others, and that their saying, "You are to me like the back of my mother," is an abominable word and a falsehood.

He also made clear the expiation (kaffārah) required in this case upon return (ʿawd), in His saying: ﴿Those of you who make zihar from their wives—they are not their mothers. Their mothers are only those who bore them. And indeed, they utter an abominable word and falsehood. And indeed, Allah is Pardoning and Forgiving.﴾ ﴿And those who make zihar from their wives and then go back on what they said—then (the expiation is) the freeing of a slave before they touch one another. That is what you are admonished to do, and Allah is Acquainted with what you do.﴾ ﴿But whoever does not find (a slave), then fasting for two consecutive months before they touch one another. But whoever is not able, then feeding sixty needy persons. That is that you may believe in Allah and His Messenger. And these are the limits set by Allah, and for the disbelievers is a painful punishment.﴾ (Q. 58:2–4).

So His saying in this verse of al-Aḥzāb: ﴿Nor has He made your wives whom you divorce by zihar your mothers﴾ is like His saying in Sūrat al-Mujādilah: ﴿Those of you who make zihar from their wives—they are not their mothers. Their mothers are only those who bore them﴾. You have seen what is in Sūrat al-Mujādilah of addition and clarification of what this verse of al-Aḥzāb contains.

* *

Issues related to this noble verse

The first issue: You have learned from the Qur'an that undertaking zihar against a wife is forbidden with severe prohibition, as His saying indicates: ﴿And indeed, they utter an abominable word and falsehood﴾. Since Allah, may He be exalted, has explicitly stated that it is abominable and false, its prohibition is severe, as you see. He showed that it is a lie and falsehood by His saying: ﴿They are not their mothers. Their mothers are only those who bore them﴾, and His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Allah has not made for any man two hearts within his body, nor has He made your wives whom you divorce by zihar your mothers﴾.

By His saying: ﴿And indeed, Allah is Pardoning and Forgiving﴾, He indicated that whoever has committed the abominable zihar and its falsehood, if he repents to Allah from that with sincere repentance (tawbah naṣūḥ), Allah forgives him that abomination and falsehood and pardons him. Glory be to Him, how generous He is and how forbearing!

* *

The second issue: On clarifying the "return" (ʿawd) upon which Allah made the expiation obligatory, in His saying: ﴿then go back on what they said—then the freeing of a slave before they touch one another﴾, and removing a problem in the verse.

Know that this issue we have explained in our book "Daf' Iham al-Iḍṭirāb ʿan Āyāt al-Kitāb" (Removing the Appearance of Contradiction from the Verses of the Book), and here we will mention what we said there, to complete the benefit.

In "Daf' Iham al-Iḍṭirāb" there is the following text: His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And those who make zihar from their wives and then go back on what they said—then the freeing of a slave before they touch one another﴾. It is not hidden that His ordering the expiation by manumission upon zihar and return together implies that the expiation is obligatory only with zihar and return together. And His saying: ﴿before they touch one another﴾ is explicit that the expiation must occur before returning to touching.

Know first: what Ibn Ḥazm preferred from the view of Dāwūd al-Ẓāhirī, and which Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr related from Bukayr ibn al-Ashajj, al-Farrāʾ and a group of theologians, and which Shuʿbah held: that the meaning of ﴿then go back on what they said﴾ is their returning to the wording of zihar, so that they repeat it a second time, is a false view, as evidenced by the fact that the Prophet ﷺ did not ask for details (lam yastafṣil) from the woman concerning whom the verse of zihar was revealed, whether her husband repeated the formula of zihar or not. And leaving out such inquiry (tark al-istifṣāl) takes the place of generality in statements, as has been mentioned repeatedly.

The verification (taḥqīq) is: the expiation and the prohibition of intercourse before it do not require repetition of the formula of zihar. And what some have claimed also, that the speech contains inversion (taqdīm and taʾkhīr), and that its intended sense is: "And those who make zihar from their wives, then go back on what they said, then the freeing of a slave before they touch one another, free from sin by means of the expiation," is also not sound, because it is established in the principles of jurisprudence that the sequence must be preserved unless there is evidence. To this refers the saying of the author of Marāqī al-Suʿūd:

"Likewise sequence is for making obligatory the action that has the stronger probability among what is possible."

We will mention, Allah willing, the answer to this problem according to the views of the four Imams, may Allah be pleased with them all.

So we say, and in Allah we seek help: the meaning of ʿawd according to Mālik has two views, and the Mudawwanah has been interpreted in accordance with each of them, and both are preferred.

The first: it is the resolve (ʿazm) upon intercourse only.

The second: it is the resolve upon intercourse and keeping the wife together.

On both views there is no problem in the verse. For the meaning then is: "And those who make zihar from their wives, then resolve upon intercourse, or upon it together with keeping (the wife), then the freeing of a slave before they touch one another." There is no contradiction between the resolve upon intercourse, or upon it with keeping, and manumission before touching.

The most that this view requires is the omission of the word "intention" (irādah), which occurs in the Qur'an, as in His saying: ﴿When you intend to stand up for prayer﴾ (Q. 5:6), meaning, "when you intend to rise to it," and His saying: ﴿So when you recite the Qur'an﴾ (Q. 16:98), meaning, "when you intend to recite it, seek refuge in Allah" (Q. 16:98).

The meaning of ʿawd according to al-Shāfiʿī is that he keeps her after the zihar for a period of time in which he could divorce her but does not divorce. On this too there is no problem in the verse, because his keeping her for the said period does not contradict expiation before touching, as is clear.

The meaning of ʿawd according to Aḥmad is that he returns to intercourse or resolves upon it. As for resolve, we have shown there is no problem in the verse on the view of it. As for the view that it is intercourse:

Then the answer is: if he made zihar and had intercourse before expiation, it becomes obligatory for him to refrain from touching again until he expiates, and it does not follow from this that the first intercourse before expiation was permissible, because the verse according to this view only clarifies the ruling where intercourse occurred before expiation, and that expiation is obligatory before another touching. As for undertaking the first touching, its prohibition is known from the generality of His saying: ﴿before they touch one another﴾.

The meaning of ʿawd according to Abū Ḥanīfah, may Allah the Exalted have mercy on him, is resolve upon intercourse, and on this there is no problem, as already mentioned. What the Ḥāfiẓ Ibn Kathīr, may Allah the Exalted have mercy on him, related in his tafsir from Mālik, that he said ʿawd is intercourse, is contrary to what is known of his school; likewise what he related from Abū Ḥanīfah, that ʿawd is returning to zihar after its prohibition and after the removal of what was the pre-Islamic practice, is contrary to what is established in the Ḥanafī positive law (furūʿ), which is that it is resolve upon intercourse, as we have mentioned. Most of what has been said about the meaning of ʿawd returns to the views of the Imams that we have mentioned, may Allah have mercy on them.

Some scholars said: what is meant by ʿawd is returning to enjoyment (istimtāʿ) without intercourse, and what is meant by touching (masīs) in His saying: ﴿before they touch one another﴾ is specifically intercourse, and on this there is no problem. The lack of clarity of this view is not hidden.

The verification: enjoyment through intercourse or other than it is not permissible before expiation, because of the generality of His saying: ﴿before they touch one another﴾. Some permitted enjoyment other than intercourse, saying: the intended meaning of touching in His saying ﴿before they touch one another﴾ is intercourse itself, not its preliminaries. Among those who said so: al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī, al-Thawrī, and it was narrated from al-Shāfiʿī in one of his two views.

Some scholars said: the lām in His saying ﴿for what they said﴾ means "in", i.e., they return in what they said, meaning they go back on it; as in the Prophet's ﷺ saying: "The one who takes back his gift is like the dog that returns to its vomit" (the ḥadīth), and it was said: the lām means "from", i.e., they return from what they said, meaning they retract it, and this is close to what came before.

The author of these notes, may Allah pardon him and forgive him, says: What appears to me, and Allah knows best, is that ʿawd has a beginning and an end. Its beginning is the resolve upon intercourse, and its end is actual intercourse. So whoever resolves upon intercourse has returned by intention, and the expiation becomes obligatory for him in order to make intercourse permissible; and whoever has intercourse in fact, the obligation becomes binding upon him, and he has violated by undertaking intercourse before expiation.

This is indicated by the Prophet's ﷺ saying when he said: "When two Muslims meet with their swords, the killer and the killed are in the Fire." They said: "O Messenger of Allah, we understand the killer; but what of the killed?" He said: "He was eager to kill his companion." So he made clear that resolving upon an act is a deed for which a person is held accountable.

If it is said: the apparent and immediate meaning of the verse agrees with the view of the Ẓāhiriyyah, whose invalidity we have already mentioned, because the apparent immediate meaning of His saying ﴿for what they said﴾ is the formula of zihar, so return to it would be repeating it a second time.

(p-193) The answer is: the meaning of "for what they say" (li-ma qalu) is that it is forbidden for them, namely intercourse. This is supported by the existence of a parallel to it in the Qur'an, in the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And We will inherit from him what he says﴾ [Maryam: 80], meaning what he claims he will be given of wealth and children, in His words: ﴿I will surely be given wealth and children﴾ [Maryam: 77]. And what we have mentioned, that whoever has intercourse before the expiation is obliged to refrain from touching (the wife) once more until he makes expiation, is the sound position, contrary to those who said: the expiation falls away through intercourse before touching, as is narrated from al-Zuhri, Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Abu Yusuf; and contrary to those who said: two expiations become obligatory by it, as is narrated from Abdullah ibn Amr ibn al-As, and some have mentioned it from Amr ibn al-As and Abd al-Rahman ibn Mahdi; and contrary to those who said: three expiations become obligatory upon him, as narrated by Sa'id ibn Mansur from al-Hasan and Ibrahim. And Allah knows best. End of the lengthy quotation from "Daf' Iham al-Idtirab 'an Ayat al-Kitab."

* *

The third issue: The stronger of the two opinions of the scholars in my view is that if he says to her: "You are to me like the back of my daughter," or "my sister," or "my paternal aunt," or "my grandmother," or "my mother," or "my milk-mother," or "my milk-sister," or he likens her to another body part other than the back, such as saying: "You are to me like the head of my daughter or sister," etc., or the belly of any of those mentioned, or her private part, or her thigh, that all of this is zihar (dhihar), since there is no difference in meaning between it and "You are to me like the back of my mother," because in all of that he has likened his wife to someone who is permanently forbidden to him, like his mother, so the meaning of zihar is definitely realized in that.

Ibn Qudamah said in "al-Mughni": This is the view of most scholars, among them: al-Hasan, Ata', Jabir ibn Zayd, al-Sha'bi, al-Nakha'i, al-Zuhri, al-Thawri, al-Awza'i, Malik, Ishaq, Abu Ubayd, Abu Thawr, the people of opinion (Ashab al-Ra'y), and it is the new (jadid) of the two opinions of al-Shafi'i. In the older (qadim) opinion he said: zihar occurs only with a mother or a grandmother, because she is also a mother; because the wording with which the Qur'an came is specific to the mother, so if one departs from it, what Allah the Exalted made obligatory in it does not apply. Our argument is that they are all forbidden by kinship, so they are like the mother. As for the verse, it says: ﴿And indeed they say an objectionable word and falsehood﴾, and this exists in our issue, so it takes its ruling, and attaching the ruling to the mother does not prevent its establishment for others when they are similar to her. End of the quotation from "al-Mughni," and it is clear, as you see.

The third category: that he likens her to the back of one who is permanently forbidden to him other than relatives, such as nursing mothers, milk-sisters, the wives of fathers and sons, the mothers of wives, and the stepdaughters whose mothers he has consummated marriage with. Then it is also zihar, and the disagreement regarding them is like that regarding the previous one, and the reasoning of the two positions (p-194) is as previously stated. It adds regarding nursing mothers that they are included in the general term "mothers," so they are within the text, and the rest of them are in its meaning, so its ruling applies to them. End of quotation from "al-Mughni," and it is clear, as you see.

* *

Two branches relate to this issue.

The first: Know that the scholars differed regarding the case where he likens his wife to the back of one who is forbidden to him temporarily, such as her sister or her paternal aunt, or a non-related woman. Some scholars said: it is zihar, and this is the view of the companions of Malik, who regard it as a type of clear metaphor (kinaya zahira). It is one of the two narrations from Ahmad, and al-Khiraqi chose it. The other narration from Ahmad is that it is not zihar, and this is the position of Abu Hanifa and al-Shafi'i.

The argument of the first view: he likened his wife to a forbidden woman, so it is like if he likened her to the mother, because all share in the prohibition; since the mere saying "You are forbidden to me" (anti 'alayya haram), if he intends zihar by it, is zihar according to the more apparent view, and likening to a forbidden woman is prohibition, so it is zihar.

The argument of the second view: the one he likened his wife to is not permanently forbidden, so she does not have the ruling of the mother's back unless her prohibition is permanent like the mother's. Since her prohibition is not permanent, likening to her is not zihar, as if he likened her to the back of a menstruating woman or of one of his wives in ihram. Those who disagreed answered this: mere likening to a forbidden woman suffices for zihar, as it falls under the general meaning of His words: ﴿And indeed they say an objectionable word and falsehood﴾. They said: as for the menstruating woman, enjoyment of her is permissible other than the private part, and for the woman in ihram it is permissible for him to look at her and touch her without desire, and there is no prescribed penalty for intercourse with either of them, unlike our issue. End of quotation from "al-Mughni," with slight editing that does not affect the meaning.

The author of "al-Mughni" said: Abu Bakr chose that zihar occurs only with women who are permanently unlawful (dhawat al-mahram) among women. He said: "On this I say."

Some scholars said: if he likens his wife to the back of a non-related woman, it is a divorce. This was said by some Malikis. (End.)

The author of this commentary, may Allah pardon him and forgive him, says: The most apparent of the views of the scholars in my opinion, and the most consistent with the principles, is the view of the one who says he is a zahir (one making zihar), even if the woman he likened his wife to is not permanently forbidden, since permanence of prohibition is not necessary; the basis of zihar is the prohibition of the wife through likening her to a forbidden woman, and this is achieved by likening her to a woman who is forbidden at the present time, even if temporarily, since the prohibition of the wife is achieved by that according to the man's intention. And Allah knows best.

* *

The second branch: Regarding the ruling on his saying to her: "You are to me like the back of my father, or my son, or others of men." I know of no text from the Book or the Sunnah on this, and the scholars differ on it. Some said: he does not become a zahir by that. Ibn Qudamah said in "al-Mughni": This is the view of most scholars, because it is a likening to something that is not a place for enjoyment, so it is like saying "You are to me like the wealth of Zayd." Is there expiation in it? There are two narrations:

One: there is expiation in it, because it is a type of prohibition, so it is like if he prohibited his property.

The second: there is nothing in it. Ibn al-Qasim narrated from Ahmad, regarding one who likens his wife to the back of a man, that it is not zihar, and I have not seen that anything is required in it, because it is a likening of his wife to something that is not a place for enjoyment, similar to likening her to the property of another. Some said: he becomes a zahir by likening to the back of a man. This is attributed in "al-Mughni" to Ibn al-Qasim, companion of Malik, and Jabir ibn Zayd. There are two narrations from Ahmad, like the two positions mentioned, and that this is zihar is the well-known view among later Malikis.

The author of this commentary, may Allah pardon him and forgive him, says: What appears is that this issue fits a principle of usul al-fiqh in which the usulists have three positions, concerning when a wording falls between the customary meaning (al-haqiqa al-'urfiyya) and the linguistic meaning (al-haqiqa al-lughawiyya): which is it to be understood as? The correct view according to a group of usulists is that the wording is understood first as its legal meaning (al-haqiqa al-shar'iyya) if it has one; then if it has no legal meaning, it is understood as its customary meaning, then its linguistic meaning.

From Abu Hanifa: it is understood as its linguistic meaning before its customary meaning. He said: because the customary meaning, though it has gained preference through predominance of usage, the linguistic meaning is preferred by the original coinage.

The third view: neither is given precedence over the other; rather it is judged that both are equal, so the wording is mujmal (ambiguous) because the two possibilities are equal, and it needs to be clarified which of the two possibilities is intended by intention or external evidence. To this question the author of "Maraqi al-Su'ud" alluded, saying:

"The wording is understood as the legal meaning if there is one, otherwise the general customary meaning,
Then the linguistic meaning is understood as the clear one, and there is no need to search for a metaphor in what is chosen,
And the view of al-Nu'man is the reverse of what passed, and the view of ambiguity in it is accepted."

Knowing this, know that a man's saying to his wife, "You are to me like the back of my father," for example, does not in customary usage refer to enjoyment through intercourse or its preliminaries, because custom does not include enjoyment of males, so there is no zihar in it. But if the linguistic meaning is given precedence, then the absolute likening of the wife to a mahram, even a male, requires prohibition, so by linguistic meaning it has the ruling of zihar. The apparent view is that his saying "You are to me like carrion and blood, and like the back of an animal," and similar things, like his saying "You are to me like the back of my father," fall under the same ruling. And Allah knows best.

* *

The fourth issue: Know that a man's saying to his wife, "You are forbidden to me" (anti 'alayya haram), or "If you enter the house, then you are forbidden," and then she enters it, has around twenty opinions among the scholars, as is known in its proper place.

This verse of zihar indicates that the most analogical of the opinions and the closest to the apparent meaning of the Qur'an is the view of the one who says: the prohibition of the wife is zihar, for which the expiation of zihar is obligatory, and it is not divorce.

The clarification of this: his saying "You are to me like the back of my mother" means "You are forbidden to me," and Allah the Exalted has explicitly stated the obligation of expiation in the saying "You are to me like the back of my mother." And it is not hidden that "You are forbidden to me" is similar to it in meaning, as you see.

In "al-Mughni" it says: Ibrahim al-Harbi mentioned from Uthman, Ibn Abbas, Abu Qilaba, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Maymun ibn Mihran, and al-Batti that they said: prohibition is zihar. (End.) The closest of the views after this to the apparent meaning of the Qur'an is the view that there is expiation of oath, and seeking forgiveness, based on His words: ﴿Allah has already ordained for you the dissolution of your oaths﴾ [al-Tahrim: 2], and His words: ﴿And Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾ [al-Tahrim: 1], after His words: ﴿Why do you prohibit﴾ [al-Tahrim: 1], the verse.

* *

The fifth issue: The more apparent view is that his saying "You are with me, or from me, or beside me, like the back of my mother" has no difference from his saying "You are to me like the back of my mother." It is zihar, as many have said, and it is clear, as you see.

* *

The sixth issue: The most apparent of the views of scholars in my opinion, regarding one who says to his wife, "You are to me like my mother, or like the likeness of my mother," without mentioning the back, is that it is not zihar unless he intends zihar by it, because the wording has possible meanings other than zihar, even though its usage in those meanings is well known. If he says, "I intended by it zihar," then it is zihar according to the consensus of the scholars, as stated in "al-Mughni." If he intended by it that she is like her in honor and reverence to him, or that she is like her in age or attribute, then it is not zihar, and the statement is his in regard to his intention, as stated in "al-Mughni."

As for if he intended nothing, Ibn Qudamah said in "al-Mughni": If he uses it absolutely, Abu Bakr said: it is explicit in zihar, and this is the view of Malik and Muhammad ibn al-Hasan. Ibn Abi Musa said: there are two narrations on it, the more apparent of which is that it is not zihar until he intends it. This is the view of Abu Hanifa and al-Shafi'i, because this wording is used more for honor than for prohibition, so it is not directed to it without intention, like the metaphors of divorce. (End of quotation.)

The author of this commentary, may Allah pardon him and forgive him, says: This view is the most apparent to me, because the wording mentioned is not specified either by custom or by linguistic meaning, except by an indicator showing that he intended zihar.

Ibn Qudamah said in "al-Mughni": The basis of the first view, that this is zihar, is that he likened his wife to his mother as a whole, so he was likening her to her back, and zihar is established, just as if he had likened her to it alone.

The position that is most sound to me, according to the analogical reasoning of the school (madhhab), is this: if there is an indication (qarīnah) that points to ẓihār (the pre-Islamic pronouncement of likening one's wife to one's mother's back, which makes her unlawful to the husband), such as his phrasing it as an oath, saying, "If you do such-and-such, then you are to me like my mother," or if he says it during a quarrel and anger, then it is ẓihār. This is because, when a statement takes the form of an oath, the oath is meant to restrain from something or to urge toward something, and this is achieved only by making her unlawful to him. Moreover, her being like his mother in her qualities or her honor is not contingent upon a condition, which indicates that he intended ẓihār. The occurrence of the statement in a state of quarrel and anger is evidence that he meant by it what relates to harming her and requires keeping away from her, which is ẓihār. If this indication is absent, then it is not ẓihār, because the statement admits of meanings other than ẓihār to a great degree, so ẓihār cannot be fixed as its meaning without evidence. A similar view is that of Abū Thawr. This is the end of the relevant point from al-Mughnī, and it is the more apparent view, so one should not turn away from it. And knowledge is with Allah, exalted is He.

* *

The seventh issue: the view most apparent to me among the scholars is that if he says, "Lawful is unlawful to me," or "What Allah has made lawful is unlawful to me," or "What has become lawful to me is unlawful," and he has a wife, then he is a ẓāhir (one who pronounces ẓihār), because the wife falls under the general scope of these expressions.

In al-Mughnī he said: Aḥmad explicitly stated this in the three cases. End of quote. And this is apparent.

This is according to the most analogically sound view, namely that such prohibition is ẓihār. And the more apparent of the two views in my opinion regarding one who says, "What Allah has made lawful of family and property is unlawful to me," is that ẓihār is binding on him, along with what is binding in prohibiting what Allah has made lawful of property. That is, a kaffārah of oath (kaffārat yamīn) according to those who hold this, so he is bound by the kaffārah of ẓihār and the kaffārah of oath.

(p-198) This which we have found more apparent is the view chosen by Ibn ʿAqīl, in contrast to what is transmitted in al-Mughnī from Aḥmad and supported there, that the kaffārah of ẓihār suffices in place of the kaffārah of oath. And knowledge is with Allah, exalted is He.

* *

The eighth issue: the most apparent view among the scholars in my opinion, regarding one who says to his wife, "You are unlawful to me like the back of my mother," or "You are to me like the back of my mother, unlawful," is that he is a ẓāhir absolutely, and it does not refer to divorce, even if he intended it, because the wording is explicit in ẓihār.

* *

The ninth issue: the most apparent view among the scholars in my opinion, regarding one who says to his wife, "You are divorced like the back of my mother," is that if the divorce is irrevocable (bāʾin), she becomes separated by it, and no ẓihār occurs by his saying "like the back of my mother," because his utterance of that took place when she was a non-wife (ajnabiyyah), so it is like ẓihār from a non-wife. If the divorce is revocable (raj'iyy), and he intended by "like the back of my mother" ẓihār, he is a ẓāhir, because a revocably divorced woman is a wife to whom both ẓihār and divorce apply. If he did not intend ẓihār by it, then it is not ẓihār, because he used the explicit term of divorce first and made his saying "like the back of my mother" a description of it, and the explicit term of divorce does not refer to ẓihār.

In al-Mughnī, he transmitted this view that we have found more apparent from al-Qāḍī and said: It is the position of al-Shāfiʿī.

As for if he puts ẓihār before divorce, saying, "You are to me like the back of my mother, divorced," then the more apparent view is that both ẓihār and divorce occur together, whether the divorce is irrevocable or revocable, because ẓihār does not remove the marital bond, and separation does not occur through it, since the kaffārah removes its ruling, so it does not prevent divorce from taking effect upon the one who pronounced ẓihār on her. And knowledge is with Allah, exalted is He.

* *

The tenth issue: the most apparent view among the scholars in my opinion is that if he likens any part of his wife to his mother's back, or to any of her parts, then he is a ẓāhir, because the meaning of making the wife unlawful is achieved thereby. Whether the mother's part is one that it is permissible for him to look at, such as her head and hand, or one that is not permissible for him to look at, such as her private part and thigh, is equal. This is the view of Mālik, al-Shāfiʿī, and one of the two narrations from Aḥmad. There is another narration: that he is not a ẓāhir until he likens her whole body, because if he swears by Allah that he will not touch a specific part of her, he does not extend it to other parts of her, so likewise with ẓihār. And because this is neither explicitly stated nor in the meaning of what is explicitly stated. And from Abū Ḥanīfah: if he likens her to what it is forbidden to look at from the mother, such as the thigh and the private part, then it is ẓihār, and if he likens her to what it is permissible to look at, such as the hand and the head, then it is not ẓihār, because likening her to a part that is lawful to look at is like likening her to a part of another wife of his, so ẓihār is not achieved thereby.

We have found it more apparent that it is ẓihār absolutely, because the meaning of prohibition is achieved by it, so it is in the meaning of explicit ẓihār. Therefore their statement, "it is not in the meaning of what is explicitly stated," is not accepted; rather, it is in its meaning. And analogizing it to his oath by Allah that he will not touch a specific part of her is clearly invalid, because the meaning of prohibition is achieved by a part, and an oath concerning one part does not extend to another part, as you see. And Abū Ḥanīfah's statement, that ẓihār is not achieved by likening to a part that is lawful to look at, is also not accepted, because although looking at it is permitted, enjoying it is forbidden, and enjoyment is what is obtained from the marriage contract. So likening to it necessarily entails prohibition, and ẓihār is itself the prohibition by means of likening to the forbidden part of the mother.

Know that the view that ẓihār occurs by saying, "Your hair, or your saliva, or your speech is to me like the back of my mother," has a strong basis in reasoning, because hair is among the beauties of women by which husbands enjoy themselves, as we explained in the surah of al-Ḥajj. Likewise saliva, for the husband sucks it and enjoys it from his wife. Likewise speech, as is well known. As for if he says to her, "Your coughing, or your spitting, or the like, is to me like the back of my mother," then the apparent view is that this is nothing, because coughing and spitting, and what goes in their direction, like tears, are not things one ordinarily enjoys. And knowledge is with Allah, exalted is He.

* *

The eleventh issue: the scholars differed regarding one who says to his female slave (amah), "You are to me like the back of my mother," or says that to the mother of his child (umm walad). Some scholars said: ẓihār is not valid from a female slave. This is transmitted from Ibn ʿUmar, ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAmr, Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyab, Mujāhid, al-Shaʿbī, Rabīʿah, al-Awzāʿī, al-Shāfiʿī, Abū Ḥanīfah and his companions, and Aḥmad. Others said: ẓihār is valid from a slave-woman, whether she is an umm walad or not. This is the view of Mālik, and it is also transmitted from al-Ḥasan, ʿIkrimah, al-Nakhaʿī, ʿAmr ibn Dīnār, Sulaymān ibn Yasār, al-Zuhrī, al-Ḥakam, al-Thawrī, and Qatādah, and it is one narration from Aḥmad. And from al-Ḥasan and al-Awzāʿī: if he has intercourse with her, it is ẓihār, and otherwise it is not. And from ʿAṭāʾ: if he pronounces ẓihār from his slave-woman, he is bound by half the kaffārah of ẓihār that applies to a free wife.

Those who said that ẓihār is not valid from a slave-woman argued with evidence. Among it, they claimed that the words, "Those who pronounce ẓihār from their wives," (﴿يُظاهِرُونَ مِن نِسائِهِمْ﴾) are specific to wives, not to concubines.

Among it, ẓihār is a statement by which the prohibition of a wife is effected, so a slave-woman does not enter it, by analogy with divorce.

Among it, ẓihār was a form of divorce in the pre-Islamic period; its ruling was transferred, but its object remained, and the object of divorce is wives, not concubines.

Among it, the prohibition of a slave-woman is a prohibition of something lawful from his property, so there is a kaffārah of oath in it, like the prohibition of the rest of his property, according to one who holds that prohibiting property entails a kaffārah of oath, as has preceded in the surah of al-Ḥajj.

They said: among it, the Prophet ﷺ prohibited his slave-girl Māriyah, and no ẓihār was binding on him, but only a kaffārah of oath, as Allah said regarding his prohibition of her: ﴿O Prophet, why do you prohibit what Allah has made lawful for you?﴾ [al-Taḥrīm: 1], then He said: ﴿Allah has already ordained for you the dissolution of your oaths﴾ [al-Taḥrīm: 2], to the end of the verse.

Those who held that ẓihār from a slave-woman is valid argued by her inclusion in the general scope of His saying, "And those who pronounce ẓihār from their wives," (﴿والَّذِينَ يُظاهِرُونَ مِن نِسائِهِمْ﴾). They said: their slave-women are among their wives, because their enjoyment of their slave-women is part of their enjoyment of their wives. They said: and because a slave-woman is permissible for intercourse, like a wife, so ẓihār is valid from her, like a wife. They said: and His saying, "O Prophet, why do you prohibit," was revealed concerning his prohibition of drinking honey, in the well-known story, not concerning the prohibition of the slave-girl.

The argument of al-Ḥasan and al-Awzāʿī, and the argument of ʿAṭāʾ, are both clear, as preceded.

Ibn al-ʿArabī the Mālikī said, regarding Mālik's view and that of his companions that ẓihār from a slave-woman is valid: this is a difficult issue for us, because Mālik says that if he says to his slave-woman, "You are unlawful to me," it does not bind him; so how can the explicit wording of prohibition be void in her case while its allusive wording is valid? But the slave-woman enters the general scope of His saying, "from their wives" (﴿مِن نِسائِهِمْ﴾), because He meant "from those lawful to them."

The reasoning in it is that it is a statement which relates to intercourse without dissolving the marriage contract, so it is valid regarding a slave-woman, its origin being an oath by Allah, exalted is He. End of his words, through the transmission of al-Qurṭubī.

The author of this commentary, may Allah pardon him and forgive him, says: It is not far-fetched, according to the principles of legal theory and what is established in the sciences of the Qur'an, that there is a distinction between the prohibition of a slave-woman and the prohibition of a wife.

The clarification of this: His saying, exalted is He, "Why do you prohibit what Allah has made lawful for you," came in some authentic narrations in the Sunan and elsewhere, that it was revealed concerning the Prophet ﷺ prohibiting his slave-girl Māriyah, mother of Ibrāhīm. Although it came in the narrations established in the two Ṣaḥīḥs that it was revealed concerning his prohibition of the honey he had drunk at the house of one of his wives, and the story of that is famous and authentic, because what is established in the sciences of the Qur'an is that when it is established that a verse was revealed concerning a specific matter, and then it is established by another authentic chain that it was revealed concerning another specific matter other than the first, it is obligatory to interpret it as having been revealed concerning both together, so it has two occasions of revelation, like the revelation of the verse of mutual cursing (li'ān) concerning ʿUwaymir and Hilāl together.

And by this you know that it must be said that His saying, exalted is He, "O Prophet, why do you prohibit what Allah has made lawful for you," etc., was revealed concerning his ﷺ prohibiting honey upon himself, and concerning his prohibiting his slave-girl. When you know this about the revelation of "why do you prohibit" concerning the prohibition of the slave-girl, you know that the Qur'an indicates that prohibiting the slave-girl does not make her unlawful, and it is not ẓihār from her, and that a kaffārah of oath is binding in it, as is authentically reported from Ibn ʿAbbās and those who agreed with him. Ibn ʿAbbās said: when He made clear that there is a kaffārah of oath in it, He said, "Indeed, in the Messenger of Allah you have an excellent example" (﴿لَقَدْ كانَ لَكم في رَسُولِ اللَّهِ أُسْوَةٌ حَسَنَةٌ﴾) [al-Aḥzāb: 21]. Its meaning is that the Prophet ﷺ made expiation for his prohibition of his slave-girl with a kaffārah of oath, because Allah, exalted is He, said, "Allah has already ordained for you the dissolution of your oaths," after his ﷺ prohibition of the aforementioned slave-girl in His saying, "Why do you prohibit what Allah has made lawful for you." As for those scholars who said that whoever prohibits his slave-girl is not bound by a kaffārah of oath, but is only bound by seeking forgiveness, they argued by His saying, exalted is He, "And Allah is Oft-Forgiving, Most Merciful," after His saying, "Why do you prohibit," and they said: "When the Prophet ﷺ prohibited his slave-girl, he said along with that, 'By Allah, I will not return to her.'" This oath is the one regarding which Allah revealed, "Allah has already ordained for you the dissolution of your oaths," and it was not revealed concerning the mere prohibition of the slave-girl. The oath mentioned together with the prohibition in the story of the slave-girl. In Nayl al-Awṭār it says: al-Ṭabarānī transmitted it with an authentic chain from Zayd ibn Aslam, the well-known Successor (tābiʿī), but he transmitted it as mursal (with a missing companion in the chain). Likewise Ibn Jarīr transmitted it from him. End of quote.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 33, verse 4 (part 4 of 7):

Ibn Kathir said in his Tafsir: Al-Haytham ibn Kulayb narrated it in his Musnad with a sound chain of narration, and he related the aforementioned chain from him, may Allah be pleased with him. The text in it mentions both the prohibition and the oath, as we have mentioned. And according to what we have mentioned, that the verse ﴿Why do you prohibit what Allah has made lawful for you?﴾ was revealed concerning his ﷺ prohibiting his slave-girl (ﷺ), then the difference between prohibiting a slave-girl and prohibiting a wife is evident. For the verse ﴿Why do you prohibit﴾ indicates that prohibiting a slave-girl does not make her forbidden and is not a zihar (zihar: a pre-Islamic form of divorce in which a husband likens his wife to his mother's back). And the verse ﴿And those who divorce by zihar from their wives and then retract what they have said - then the freeing of a slave﴾ to the end of the verse indicates that prohibiting a wife requires the expiation of zihar stated in al-Mujadilah, because the meaning of ﴿who divorce by zihar from their wives﴾ in all the recitations is that one of them says to his wife: "You are to me like the back of my mother," and there is no disagreement about this. And his saying "You are to me like the back of my mother" means: "You are forbidden to me," as has been explained previously.

On this basis, the verse of "Prohibition" indicates the ruling on prohibiting a slave-girl, and the verse of "al-Mujadilah" indicates the ruling on prohibiting a wife, and these are two different rulings, (p-202) as you see. It is known that Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with both of them) did not say that there is a difference between them; rather he said: the ruling on prohibiting a wife is like the ruling on prohibiting a slave-girl, which is stated in the verse of "Prohibition." We say: the verse of zihar indicates by its implication that prohibiting a wife is zihar, because "You are to me like the back of my mother" and "You are to me forbidden" have one meaning, as is not hidden. On the basis of what we have mentioned, zihar from a slave-girl is not valid, and prohibiting her with zihar, or with explicit prohibition, requires the expiation of an oath, or seeking forgiveness, as has been mentioned previously. This is closer to the apparent meaning of the Qur'an, although many scholars hold a view contrary to it.

We have previously mentioned that there are twenty opinions among the scholars concerning a man's prohibition of his wife, and we will mention them here briefly and clarify what appears to us to be preferred by evidence from among them, if Allah the Exalted wills.

The first opinion: that a man's prohibition of his wife is void and invalid, and nothing follows from it. Ibn al-Qayyim said in I'lam al-Muwaqqi'in: This is one of the two narrations from Ibn 'Abbas, and Masruq, Abu Salamah ibn 'Abd al-Rahman, 'Ata', al-Sha'bi, Dawud, all the people of the literal (zahiriyyah) school, and most of the people of hadith held it, and it is one of the two opinions of the Malikis, adopted by Asbagh ibn al-Faraj. In the Sahih, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, that he heard Ibn 'Abbas say: "If a man prohibits his wife, it is nothing. ﴿Indeed, in the Messenger of Allah you have an excellent example﴾ [al-Ahzab: 21]." It is also authentically reported from Masruq that he said: "I do not care whether I prohibit my wife or a bowl of thareed." And it is authentically reported from al-Sha'bi concerning the prohibition of a woman: "It is less significant to me than my sandal." Abu Salamah said: "I do not care whether I prohibit my wife or prohibit the water of the river." Al-Hajjaj ibn Minhal said: A man made his wife forbidden to himself, and he asked Humayd ibn 'Abd al-Rahman about that, and Humayd said: Allah the Exalted says: ﴿So when you are free, then strive, and to your Lord turn [your] desire﴾ [al-Sharh: 7-8], and you are a man who plays, so go and play. End of his words.

The proponents of this view used as evidence the saying of the Exalted: ﴿And do not say, for what your tongues describe of falsehood, "This is lawful and this is unlawful," to invent lies against Allah. Indeed, those who invent lies against Allah will not succeed﴾ [al-Nahl: 116]; and His saying: ﴿O you who have believed, do not prohibit the good things which Allah has made lawful for you﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 87]; and the generality of His saying: ﴿Say, "Bring your witnesses who testify that Allah has prohibited this"; then if they testify, do not testify with them﴾ [al-An'am: 150]; and the generality of His saying: ﴿O Prophet, why do you prohibit what Allah has made lawful for you?﴾ to the end of the verse; and the generality of his ﷺ saying: "Whoever does an action that is not in accordance with our command, it is rejected." And it is known that prohibiting what Allah has made lawful is not part of our command.

(p-203) The second opinion: that prohibition is three divorces. Ibn al-Qayyim said in I'lam al-Muwaqqi'in: This was held by 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, Zayd ibn Thabit, Ibn 'Umar, al-Hasan al-Basri, and Muhammad ibn 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Layla. The Commander of the Faithful 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, judged with three in the case of 'Adi ibn Qays al-Kilabi, and said: "By Him in whose hand is my soul, if you touch her before she marries someone other than you, I will surely stone you." And he said in Zad al-Ma'ad: It is narrated from al-Hakam ibn 'Utaybah, then he said: I say: The established report from Zayd ibn Thabit and Ibn 'Umar is that in this case there is the expiation of an oath. He also mentioned in al-Zad that Ibn Hazm transmitted from 'Ali a suspension of judgment on this. The argument of this view for three is that she does not become forbidden to him except by three, so the occurrence of three is a necessary consequence of her being forbidden to him.

The third opinion: that she is forbidden to him by his prohibiting her. Ibn al-Qayyim said in I'lam al-Muwaqqi'in: This is also authentically reported from Abu Hurayrah, al-Hasan, Khilas ibn 'Amr, Jabir ibn Zayd, and Qatadah, and these did not mention divorce, but only ordered him to avoid her.

It is also authentically reported from 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him. Either he had two narrations, or he meant the prohibition of three. The argument of this view is that his wording only required prohibition, and did not address the number of divorces, so she became forbidden to him by the necessity of his prohibition.

The fourth opinion: suspension (waqf). Ibn al-Qayyim said in I'lam al-Muwaqqi'in: This is also authentically reported from the Commander of the Faithful 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, and it is the view of al-Sha'bi. The argument of this view is that prohibition is not divorce, and he does not possess the power to prohibit what is lawful; he only possesses the power to create the cause by which it becomes prohibited, which is divorce, and this is not explicit in divorce, nor is it among the terms which the Shari'ah established for prohibiting a wife. So the matter is ambiguous, and suspension is therefore required because of the ambiguity.

The fifth opinion: if he intended divorce by it, it is divorce; otherwise it is an oath. Ibn al-Qayyim said in al-I'lam: This is the view of Tawus, al-Zuhri, al-Shafi'i, and a narration from al-Hasan, end of quote.

This view is also reported from al-Nakha'i, Ishaq, Ibn Mas'ud, and Ibn 'Umar. The argument of this view is that prohibition is a metaphor (kinayah) for divorce, so if he intended divorce by it, it is divorce, and if he did not intend it, it is an oath, based on His saying the Exalted: ﴿O Prophet, why do you prohibit what Allah has made lawful for you?﴾, up to His saying the Exalted: ﴿Allah has already ordained for you the dissolution of your oaths﴾.

The sixth opinion: that if he intended three by it, then it is three; if he intended one, then it is one irrevocable (ba'inah); if he intended an oath, then it is an oath; and if he did not intend anything, it is a lie for which there is no consequence. This was said by Sufyan, and al-Nakha'i related it from his companions. The argument of this view is that the wording admits of what he intended from all of that, so he is followed in his intention.

The seventh opinion: the same as this, except that if he did not intend anything, it is an oath which he expiates. This is the view of al-Awza'i. The argument of this view is the apparent meaning of His saying the Exalted: ﴿Allah has already ordained for you the dissolution of your oaths﴾.

The eighth opinion: also similar, except that if he did not intend anything, it is one irrevocable divorce, applying the wording of prohibition. Thus Ibn al-Qayyim mentioned this view in I'lam al-Muwaqqi'in, and did not attribute it to anyone.

Sahib Nayl al-Awtar said: Ibn Hazm transmitted it from Ibrahim al-Nakha'i.

The ninth opinion: that in it is the expiation of zihar. Ibn al-Qayyim said in I'lam al-Muwaqqi'in: This is also authentically reported from Ibn 'Abbas, Abu Qilabah, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Wahb ibn Munabbih, and 'Uthman al-Batti, and it is one of the narrations from Imam Ahmad. The argument of this view is that Allah the Exalted made the comparison of a woman to his mother, who is forbidden to him, zihar, and made it a munkar speech and falsehood. So if comparison to a forbidden woman makes him one who has committed zihar, then if he explicitly declares her forbidden, he is more deserving of zihar. This is the most analogical and most jurisprudentially sound of the opinions. It is supported by the fact that Allah did not give the responsible person the power to prohibit or make lawful; that belongs to Allah the Exalted alone, and He gave him only the performance of actions and statements upon which prohibition and permission are consequent. So the cause is attributed to the servant and its ruling belongs to Allah the Exalted. When he says, "You are to me like the back of my mother," or says, "You are to me forbidden," he has spoken a munkar speech and falsehood, and he has lied, for Allah did not make her like the back of his mother, nor did He make her forbidden to him. So by this speech of munkar and falsehood he has obligated upon himself the more severe of the two expiations, which is the expiation of zihar.

The tenth opinion: that it is one single divorce. This is one of the two narrations from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, and the view of Hammad ibn Abi Sulayman, the teacher of Abu Hanifah. The argument of this view is that a divorce of prohibition does not necessitate prohibition by three; rather it is satisfied by its least number, and one is certain, so the wording is interpreted as that, because it is the certain one. It is analogous to prohibition by the completion of the waiting period.

The eleventh opinion: that he is believed regarding what he intended by it, so that he has his intention regarding the basic divorce and its number; and if he intended prohibition without divorce, then it is an expiable oath. Ibn al-Qayyim said: This is the view of al-Shafi'i.

The argument of this view is that the wording is suitable for all of that, so none of them is specified except by intention. If he intended mere prohibition, it is a restraint from her by prohibition, like his restraint by an oath, and she is not forbidden to him in either of the two cases, end of quote. It has already been mentioned that the school of al-Shafi'i is the fifth opinion.

Ibn al-Qayyim also said in Nayl al-Awtar: This is what he reported from him in Fath al-Bari; indeed Ibn al-Qayyim himself reported it from him.

The twelfth opinion: that he is believed regarding the basic divorce and its number, except that if he intended one, it is irrevocable; if he did not intend divorce, it is interpreted (mu'awwal); and if he intended a lie, it is nothing. This is the view of Abu Hanifah and his companions.

The argument of this view is that the wording admits of what he mentioned, except that if he intended one, it is irrevocable, because prohibition implies irrevocability, and it is of two kinds: minor and major; the minor is the one that is certain, so it is taken into account rather than the major. And there is another narration from him: if he intended a lie, he is believed in religious matters, but not accepted in judicial rulings; rather he is an ila'-maker, and it is not zihar in his view, whether he intended it or not; and even if he explicitly said, "I mean by it zihar," he would not be a zihar-maker. End of what is from I'lam al-Muwaqqi'in.

Al-Shawkani said in Nayl al-Awtar, after mentioning the words of Ibn al-Qayyim that we have mentioned just now, up to his saying: "and this is the view of Abu Hanifah and his companions," thus said Ibn al-Qayyim. In Fath (al-Bari) it is stated from the Hanafis that if he intended two, it is one irrevocable; and if he did not intend divorce, it is an oath, and he becomes an ila'-maker, end of quote.

The thirteenth opinion: that it is an oath, which is expiated by whatever expiates an oath. Ibn al-Qayyim said in I'lam al-Muwaqqi'in: This is authentically reported from Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, Ibn 'Abbas, 'A'ishah, Zayd ibn Thabit, Ibn Mas'ud, 'Abd Allah ibn 'Umar, 'Ikrimah, 'Ata', Makhul, Qatadah, al-Hasan, al-Sha'bi, Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, Sulayman ibn Yasar, Jabir ibn Zayd, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Nafi', al-Awza'i, Abu Thawr, and others, may Allah be pleased with them all.

The argument of this view is the apparent meaning of the Great Qur'an, for Allah the Exalted mentioned the obligation of the dissolution of oaths immediately after the prohibition of what is lawful, so it must certainly apply to it, and it is not permissible to make the dissolution of oaths apply to something other than what was mentioned before it, and what was mentioned is removed from the ruling of the dissolution for which it was intended. End of his words.

[p-206] The author, may God pardon him and forgive him, says: The apparent meaning is that Ibn al-Qayyim intended by these words that the case that gave rise to the revelation (the occasion of revelation) is definitely included, and that God's words ﴿God has already ordained for you the dissolution of your oaths﴾ were revealed concerning the prohibition of the lawful thing mentioned in God's words ﴿Why do you forbid what God has made lawful for you?﴾. He also meant that the inclusion of ﴿God has already ordained for you the dissolution of your oaths﴾ of the matter in God's words ﴿Why do you forbid what God has made lawful for you?﴾ is certain. In my view, this certainty is not free from scrutiny, because of what we have already cited from some scholars: that God's words ﴿God has already ordained for you the dissolution of your oaths﴾ were revealed concerning the Prophet's (ﷺ) oath that he would not return to what he had forbidden himself, not concerning the original prohibition itself. We have already pointed to the reports that indicate this at the beginning of this discussion.

The Fourteenth View: That it is a severe oath in which the freeing of a slave is required. Ibn al-Qayyim said: This has also been authentically reported from Ibn 'Abbas, Abu Bakr, 'Umar, Ibn Mas'ud, and a group of the Successors (tabi'un).

The evidence for this view is that, since it is a severe oath, its expiation is made more severe by making the freeing of a slave obligatory. The reason for its severity is that it includes the prohibition of what God has made lawful, and this is not in the servant's power. As for the saying of what is reprehensible and false, even if it intends a report, it is a lie in its reporting and a transgression in its swearing; therefore its expiation is made more severe by making the freeing of a slave obligatory, just as the expiation of zihar is made more severe by it, or by fasting two months, or by feeding sixty needy persons.

The Fifteenth View: That it is a divorce. Then, if the woman has not been consummated with, it is what he intended, whether one or more. If she has been consummated with, it is three. And if he intended less than that, this is one of the two reports from Malik.

The evidence for this view is that since the wording requires prohibition, its ruling must follow from it. A woman who has not been consummated with becomes prohibited by one pronouncement, while a woman who has been consummated with is not prohibited except by three.

Furthermore: in the school of Malik there are five views. This is the first of them, and it is the best known.

The second: that it is three in every case, whether he intended three or not. This was chosen by 'Abd al-Malik in his al-Mabsut.

The third: that it is a single irrevocable divorce in all cases. This was related by Ibn Khuwayz Mindad as a report from Malik.

The fourth: that it is a single revocable divorce. This is the view of 'Abd al-'Aziz ibn Abi Salama.

The fifth: that it is whatever he intended of these, absolutely, whether before or after consummation. You have already learned the reasoning behind these views. End of quotation from I'lam al-Muwaqqi'in.

The author, may God pardon him and forgive him, says: The well-known position is that the preferred views among the Malikis are two: the view of three, and the view of a single irrevocable divorce. The practice in the city of Fez has proceeded according to the obligation of a single irrevocable divorce in cases of prohibition. The composer of the Fez practice said:

A single irrevocable pronouncement in prohibition, and an oath by it, according to the custom of the region.

Then Ibn al-Qayyim said in I'lam al-Muwaqqi'in: As for the clarification of the school of al-Shafi'i, if he intended by it zihar, it is zihar. If he intended prohibition, it is a prohibition that entails only the obligation of expiation. If he intended divorce, it is divorce, and it is what he intended. If he used it without specifying, his companions have three opinions on it:

The first: that it is explicit in requiring expiation.

The second: that nothing is attached to it.

The third: that for a slave woman it is explicit in prohibition requiring expiation, while for a free woman it is an allusion (kinaya). They said: The original verse was revealed concerning a slave woman. They said: If he said, "You are prohibited to me," and then said, "I intended by it zihar" or "divorce," then Ibn al-Haddad said: It is said to him, "Specify one of the two matters, because one word cannot be both zihar and divorce at once." It was also said: He is bound by whichever of the two he began with. They said: If a man claims a right against another man, which the latter denies, and the latter says, "The food upon you is forbidden, and the intention is mine, not yours; I owe you nothing," and then the first says, "The food upon me is forbidden, and the intention in that is yours; you have nothing with me," then the intention is the intention of the one who swears, not the one who is made to swear, because intention belongs only to the one in whose hand the pronouncement lies.

Then he said: As for the clarification of the school of Imam Ahmad, it is that it is zihar in its unrestricted form, even if he did not intend it, unless he intends divorce or oath, in which case he is bound by what he intended. There is a second report from him that it is an oath in its unrestricted form, unless he intends by it divorce or zihar, in which case he is bound by what he intended.

There is also a third report from him: that it is zihar in every case. Even if he intends by it divorce or oath, it is neither an oath nor a divorce, just as if he intended divorce or oath by saying, "You are to me as the back of my mother," for both expressions are explicit in zihar. According to this report, if he attaches to it the words, "I mean by it divorce," then is it divorce or zihar? There are two reports. One is that it is zihar, just as if he said, "You are to me as the back of my mother; I mean by it divorce or prohibition," since prohibition is explicit in zihar. The other is that it is divorce, because he has explicitly stated his intention with a word that admits it, and at most it is an allusion in it. According to this report, if he says, "I mean by it a divorce," she is divorced once. If he says, "I mean by it the divorce," is she divorced three times or once? Both reports rest on whether the article (al-) in "al-talaq" denotes the genus or the totality. This is the clarification and explanation of his school. There is another view in this matter beyond all of this, which is that if he pronounces prohibition, it is zihar even if he intended divorce by it, and if he swears by it, it is an oath requiring expiation. This is the choice of Ibn Taymiyya, and the text and analogy indicate it. When he pronounces it, he has uttered a reprehensible and false statement, and he is more deserving of the expiation of zihar than one who likens his wife to a forbidden woman. When he swears by it, it is an oath among oaths, just as if he swore by the vow of pilgrimage, freeing a slave, or giving charity. This is pure analogy and jurisprudence. Do you not see that if he says, "For God upon me is that I free a slave, or make pilgrimage, or fast," it binds him? And if he says, "If I speak to so-and-so, then for God upon me is that," in the manner of an oath, it is an oath. Likewise if he says, "He is a Jew or a Christian," he has disbelieved by that. And if he says, "If he does such-and-such, then he is a Jew or a Christian," it is an oath. The consistent rule derived from this, indeed its exact parallel in every respect, is that if he says, "You are to me as the back of my mother," it is zihar. If he says, "If you do such-and-such, then you are to me as the back of my mother," it is an oath. The consistent rule also is that if he says, "You are divorced," it is divorce; if he says, "If you do such-and-such, then you are divorced," it is an oath. These are the sound, consistent principles derived from the Book, the Sunnah, and the balance (of reason), and success is from God. End of Ibn al-Qayyim's words.

The author, may God pardon him and forgive him, says: The most convincing of the views of the scholars to me, despite their number and spread, is that the prohibition is zihar, whether it is immediate or conditional. This is because a conditional divorce or zihar becomes binding upon the occurrence of the condition on which it depends, and in my view, the more apparent position is that it does not turn into an oath requiring expiation. This is also the view of the majority of scholars.

Malik said in al-Muwatta': Al-Qasim ibn Muhammad said: A man made a woman to himself like the back of his mother's back if he married her. 'Umar ibn al-Khattab commanded him that if he married her, he should not approach her until he has paid the expiation of one who has made zihar. End of quotation.

Then he said: And Malik related to me that it reached him that a man asked al-Qasim ibn Muhammad and Sulayman ibn Yasar about a man who made zihar with a woman before marrying her. They said: If he marries her, he shall not touch her until he has paid the expiation of one who has made zihar. End of quotation.

The known position of the great majority of scholars is that a conditional divorce takes effect when the condition on which it depends occurs, and likewise zihar.

As for the slave woman, the more apparent view is that in her prohibition the expiation is that of an oath, or seeking forgiveness, as the verse of Surat al-Tahrim indicates, as has been explained previously. And God knows best.

* *

The Twelfth Issue: Know that the scholars differed concerning the slave and the dhimmi (non-Muslim subject of a Muslim state): is zihar valid from them? The most convincing of their views to me in this matter is that zihar is valid from the slave, because the sound position is that he is included in the general scope of the general texts, except what a specific proof excludes from it, as has been previously explained. The poem's author in Maraqi al-Su'ud alludes to this:

The slave, the one who exists, and the disbeliever are all included in the scope of the thoughtful.

Accordingly, he is included in the general scope of God's words ﴿Those who make zihar from their wives﴾. The fact that God's words ﴿then the freeing of a neck﴾ do not apply to him does not affect this, because he is owned property and cannot free a slave, and he is included in God's words ﴿then whoever does not find, then fasting two consecutive months﴾. So the more apparent view is the validity of a slave's zihar, and that his expiation is limited to fasting, since he is unable to free a slave or feed the needy.

As for the dhimmi, his zihar is not valid, because zihar is a reprehensible and false statement which God expiates by freeing a slave, or fasting, or feeding. The dhimmi is a disbeliever, and disbelief is not expiated by freeing a slave, fasting, or feeding for the reprehensible and false statement he has committed, because disbelief is an evil deed with which no good deed benefits. And God knows best.

* *

The Thirteenth Issue: Know that the scholars differed concerning temporary zihar, such as saying, "You are to me as the back of my mother for a month," or "until the month of Ramadan has passed," for example. Some scholars said: Temporary zihar is valid, and when the time has passed, the zihar ceases, and the woman becomes lawful without expiation. He is not considered to have returned by intercourse after the time has ended.

In al-Mughni it says: This is the view of Ahmad, and it is what Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ata', Qatada, al-Thawri, Ishaq, Abu Thawr, and one of al-Shafi'i's two views said. His final view is that it is not zihar. This was the view of Ibn Abi Layla and al-Layth, because the law came with the word zihar in an unrestricted form, and this is not unrestricted; it resembles the case where he likens her to one who is forbidden to him at a certain time but not at another. Tawus said: If he makes zihar at a certain time, expiation is due upon him, even if he fulfills the condition. Malik said: The time limit drops out and it becomes unrestricted zihar, because this is a word that makes the wife forbidden, so if he limits it by time, the limit does not apply, just as in divorce.

The author, may God pardon him and forgive him, says: The view closest to the truth to me on this question is the view of the one who said that temporary zihar is valid and ends when the time expires, because there is a report from the Prophet (ﷺ) indicating this, in a hadith that al-Tirmidhi graded as hasan, and that Ibn Khuzayma and Ibn al-Jarud graded as sahih. Some of its chains are not below the level of hasan, even if 'Abd al-Haqq and others criticized some of its chains for being mursal (having a missing companion in the chain). This is because a hadith that some scholars have graded sahih is closer to the truth than a matter on which there is no text at all.

(p-210) Abu Dawud said in his *Sunan*: Uthman ibn Abi Shaybah and Muhammad ibn al-'Ala' al-Ma'ni narrated to us, both saying: Ibn Idris narrated to us, from Muhammad ibn Ishaq, from Muhammad ibn 'Amr ibn 'Ata', who said, and Ibn al-'Ala' ibn 'Alqamah ibn 'Ayyash added, from Sulayman ibn Yasar, from Salamah ibn Sakhr, who said: "Ibn al-'Ala' al-Bayadi said, he said: I was a man who had more sexual desire for women than others did. When the month of Ramadan came, I feared that I would have intercourse with my wife during the day and be unable to stop myself until morning, so I made her unlawful to me by *zihar* (a pronouncement of likening a wife to one's mother) until the month of Ramadan ended. Then one night while she was serving me, part of her body was uncovered to me, and I could not restrain myself, and I came upon her. When morning came, I went out to my people and informed them of the matter..." The narration continues at length, and in it: the Prophet (ﷺ) ordered him to free a slave. He said he could not find a slave. He was ordered to fast two consecutive months, and he said he could not. He was ordered to feed sixty poor persons, and he said likewise. Then the Prophet (ﷺ) gave him a charity of dates from his people, the Banu Zurayq, and ordered him to feed sixty poor persons with a *wasq* of it and to use the rest for himself.

The point of evidence in the hadith is that he made his *zihar* from his wife time-limited to the month of Ramadan, and he had intercourse during the very month he had set as the term of his *zihar*. This indicates that a time-limited *zihar* is valid and binding. Had its time limitation been invalid, the Prophet (ﷺ) would have explained that. And had it been that the ruling of the time limitation was perpetual and lapsed, he (ﷺ) would have explained that too, because explanation may not be delayed beyond the time of need for it.

At-Tirmidhi said in his *Jami'*: Ishaq ibn Mansur narrated to us, Harun ibn Isma'il al-Khazzaz narrated to us, 'Ali ibn al-Mubarak narrated to us, Yahya ibn Abi Kathir narrated to us, Abu Salamah and Muhammad ibn 'Abd al-Rahman narrated to us: that Salman ibn Sakhr al-Ansari, of the Banu Bayadah, made his wife unlawful to himself like the back of his mother until Ramadan passed... The narration continues. Then at-Tirmidhi said after quoting it: "This is a *hasan* (good) hadith. It is said Salman ibn Sakhr, and it is also said Salamah ibn Sakhr al-Bayadi. The practice among the people of knowledge concerning this hadith is regarding the expiation (*kaffarah*) of *zihar*," end quote.

This chain by which at-Tirmidhi transmitted this hadith is other than the chain by which Abu Dawud transmitted it, and each of them strengthens the other. The apparent view is that this isnad of at-Tirmidhi is not below the level of *hasan*. As for what they mentioned, that 'Ali ibn al-Mubarak mentioned in it had two books from Yahya ibn Abi Kathir, one heard directly and the other a *irsal* (transmission with a missing companion) report, and that the narrations of the Kufans from him contain something that does not harm the aforementioned isnad, because the transmitter from him in it, Harun ibn Isma'il al-Khazzaz, is a Basran, not a Kufan. When al-Majd (Ibn Taymiyyah) quoted in *al-Muntaqa* the hadith of Salamah ibn Sakhr mentioned, he said: "Ahmad, Abu Dawud and at-Tirmidhi narrated it, and he said: it is a *hasan* hadith." And ash-Shawkani said in *Nayl al-Awtar*: "al-Hakim also transmitted it, and Ibn Khuzaymah and Ibn al-Jarud authenticated it, though 'Abd al-Haqq criticized it on the basis of a break in the chain, and that Sulayman ibn Yasar did not meet Salamah. at-Tirmidhi transmitted this from al-Bukhari. Its isnad also contains Muhammad ibn Ishaq," end of ash-Shawkani's words.

You already know that the isnad we mentioned from at-Tirmidhi contains neither Sulayman ibn Yasar nor Ibn (p-211) Ishaq. Thus the apparent view is that the hadith is fit to be used as evidence, as at-Tirmidhi and others mentioned.

By this you know that the correct view in this question, if Allah wills, is what we have mentioned, and knowledge is with Allah, the Exalted.

* *

**The fourteenth issue:** In my view the more evident position is that if someone says, "You are unlawful to me like the back of my mother, if Allah wills," he has behaved badly, but expiation is not obligatory upon him. The exception by the will (*istithna' bil-mashi'ah*) lifts from him the ruling of expiation, just as it lifts the expiation of an oath by Allah. And knowledge is with Allah, the Exalted.

* *

**The fifteenth issue:** The more evident view is that if he or she dies, or if he divorces her before expiation, nothing is obligatory upon him. And if he returns and marries her again after the divorce, it is not lawful for him to have intercourse with her until he makes expiation, because Allah made expiation obligatory upon the one who made *zihar* before the breaking (of the vow) through returning (*al-'awd*). So he does not return except after expiation. And there is no basis, as far as appears, for the expiation falling away through divorce. Yet some people of knowledge say that if the divorce after *zihar* was irrevocable (*ba'in*), and he then married her again, no expiation is obligatory upon him. This is narrated from Qatadah. Others say that if the separation was by three divorces, and then he married her after another husband, expiation is not obligatory upon him, because it has fallen away by the major separation, just as the proponent of the previous opinion made it fall away by the minor separation. And knowledge is with Allah, the Exalted.

* *

**The sixteenth issue:** If someone makes *zihar* from all four of his wives with a single phrase, such as saying to them, "You are unlawful to me like the back of my mother," some people of knowledge say that one expiation suffices for that.

Ibn Qudamah said in *al-Mughni*: "There is no disagreement about this in the school of Ahmad, and it is the view of 'Ali, 'Umar, 'Urwah, Tawus, 'Ata', Rabi'ah, Malik, al-Awza'i, Ishaq, Abu Thawr, and ash-Shafi'i in his earlier view (*al-qadim*). al-Hasan, an-Nakha'i, az-Zuhri, Yahya al-Ansari, al-Hakam, ath-Thawri, the people of opinion (*ashab ar-ra'y*, i.e., the Hanafis), and ash-Shafi'i in his later view (*al-jadid*) said: he owes an expiation for each wife, because *zihar* and return were found with respect to each one of them, so an expiation became obligatory upon him for each one, just as if he had made *zihar* from her alone. Our evidence is the general statement of 'Umar and 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with them both, narrated from them by al-Athram, and no opponent of them is known, so it became an *ijma'* (consensus). Also, *zihar* is a statement by which expiation becomes obligatory when violated, so when it is found in relation to a group, it makes one expiation obligatory, like an oath by Allah, the Exalted. This differs from when he makes *zihar* from her with multiple statements, for each statement requires an expiation that removes it and expiates its sin. Here the statement is one, so one expiation removes its ruling and erases its sin, and no ruling remains for it." End of quotation.

(p-212) The author of this commentary, may Allah pardon and forgive him, says: The more analogical of the two views is sufficiency with one expiation, and the more cautious of them is expiating for each one of them. As for if he makes *zihar* from them with multiple statements, by saying to each one of them separately, "You are unlawful to me like the back of my mother," the more evident view is that the expiation is multiplied, because each of those statements is "an unacceptable word and a falsehood" (Qur'an 58:2), so each one requires an expiation.

Ibn Qudamah said in *al-Mughni*: "This is the view of 'Urwah and 'Ata'. Abu 'Abd Allah ibn Hamid said: the school's position is a single narration on this. al-Qadi said: the school's position in my view is what Shaykh Abu 'Abd Allah mentioned. Abu Bakr said: there is another narration on it, that one expiation suffices for him, and he chose that, and said: this which we have said is following 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, al-Hasan, 'Ata', Ibrahim, Rabi'ah, Qabisah, and Ishaq, because the expiation of *zihar* is a right of Allah, the Exalted, so it is not multiplied by the multiplication of its cause, like the *hadd* (fixed penalty). And divorce is derived from this. Our evidence is that they are repeated oaths upon distinct persons, so each one has an expiation, just as if he had expiated and then made *zihar* again. Also, they are oaths in which breaking one does not make him break the other, so one expiation does not expiate them. Also, *zihar* is a meaning that requires expiation, so the multiplicity of expiation follows the multiplicity of its objects in different subjects, like homicide. This differs from the *hadd*, for it is a punishment averted by doubts." End of quotation.

You know that the strongest of the views for us is the multiplicity of expiation in this issue. As for if he repeats *zihar* from one wife, the apparent position that one should not depart from is this: if he repeated it before expiating for the first *zihar*, one expiation suffices. If he had expiated for his first *zihar* and then made *zihar* again after the expiation, then he owes another expiation for the *zihar* that occurred after the expiation. And knowledge is with Allah, the Exalted.

* *

**The seventeenth issue:** Know that the expiation of *zihar* is the one Allah, the Exalted, explained with His saying: ﴿then the freeing of a neck﴾ up to His saying: ﴿then feeding sixty needy persons﴾ [al-Mujadilah: 3–4].

**Branches related to this issue:**

**The first branch:** Know that the people of knowledge differed concerning the "neck" in the expiation of *zihar*: is faith a condition for it or not? Some said faith is not a condition for it. So if the one who made *zihar* freed a non-Muslim protected subject (*dhimmi*) slave, for example, it suffices him. Among those who said this view were Abu Hanifah and his companions, 'Ata', ath-Thawri, an-Nakha'i, Abu Thawr, Ibn al-Mundhir, and it is one of the two narrations from Ahmad, as stated in *al-Mughni*.

The argument of the proponents of this view is that Allah, the Exalted, said in this noble verse: ﴿then the freeing of a neck﴾ and did not restrict it by faith, so whatever the unrestricted wording of the verse covers must suffice. They said: no one has the right to restrict what Allah has left unrestricted in His Book, except by a proof that must be followed. Among those who said that faith is a condition in the neck of the expiation of *zihar* were Malik, ash-Shafi'i, al-Hasan, Ishaq, Abu 'Ubaydah, and it is the apparent position of the school of Imam Ahmad, as stated in *al-Mughni*.
