Note (tanbih).

Know that in the Great Qur'an and in the language there frequently occurs the lam with a kasrah (lam al-jarr or lam al-ta'lil, here the lam of purpose), followed by a present-tense verb in the subjunctive (manṣūb) after a verb of desire (irada);

• such as His saying here: ﴿Allah only intends to remove from you the impurity﴾, the verse,

• and His saying: ﴿Allah intends to make clear to you﴾ (An-Nisa: 26),

• and His saying: ﴿They wish to extinguish the light of Allah﴾, the verse (As-Saff: 8),

and His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Allah does not intend to place upon you any hardship, but He intends to purify you﴾, along with other verses. And like the words of the poet:

"I wish to forget her remembrance, but Layla appears to me in every path."

The scholars have various opinions about this lam mentioned above. Among them: that it is a verbal (masdariyyah) lam meaning "an" (that), and this is a strange view. Among them: that it is the lam of purpose (lam kay), and the object of the verb of desire is omitted, and the estimated meaning is: "Allah only intends that He command you and forbid you, for the purpose that He remove from you the impurity." Impurity (rijs) is everything loathsome that souls recoil from, and among the most loathsome of loathsome things is disobedience to Allah, exalted is He.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 33, verse 37:

قَوْلُهُ تَعالى: ﴿وَتُخْفِي في نَفْسِكَ ما اللَّهُ مُبْدِيهِ﴾ .

Regarding His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And you were concealing within yourself that which Allah was to bring to light﴾.

We have already mentioned, in the introduction to this blessed book, that among the types of clarification (bayan) it contains is the clarification of generality (bayan al-ijmal) that arises from ambiguity in the relative clause (silat al-mawsul, the clause that completes a relative pronoun). We also mentioned that among the examples of this is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And you were concealing within yourself that which Allah was to bring to light﴾ [al-Ahzab: 37], because the clause ﴿Allah is to bring it to light﴾ is the relative clause of the relative pronoun ma. We said in the aforementioned introduction: here He left vague what the Prophet ﷺ concealed within himself and what Allah brought to light, but He indicated that what is meant by it is his ﷺ marriage to Zaynab bint Jahsh, may Allah be pleased with her, when He revealed that to him, while at that time she was under the authority of Zayd ibn Harithah. This is because his marrying her is what Allah brought to light by His saying: ﴿So when Zayd had no longer any need for her, We married her to you﴾ [al-Ahzab: 37]. This is the verified meaning of the verse, which the Qur'an indicates, and which is befitting to his ﷺ dignity.

From this you know that what many of the exegetes say, that what he ﷺ concealed within himself and what Allah brought to light was the falling of Zaynab into his heart and his love for her while she was under Zayd, and that she heard him say: "Glory be to the One who turns hearts" (ﷺ), up to the end of the story, is all without any soundness. The proof of this is that Allah did not bring to light any of that, even though He explicitly stated that He would bring to light what the Messenger of Allah ﷺ had concealed. The purpose of our words in the introduction to this blessed book ends here.

Al-Qurtubi, may Allah have mercy on him, said in his tafsir of this verse: People differed concerning the interpretation of this verse. Qatadah, Ibn Zayd, and a group of exegetes, among them al-Tabari and others, held that the Prophet ﷺ felt admiration for Zaynab bint Jahsh while she was in the wedlock of Zayd, and he was eager that Zayd would divorce her so that he himself could marry her, up to his saying: "This is what he was concealing within himself, but he adhered to what is obligatory of enjoining good, namely his saying: ﴿Keep your wife to yourself﴾ [al-Ahzab: 37]." End of quotation. There is no doubt that this view is not correct, and that it is not befitting to him ﷺ.

Al-Qurtubi also transmitted something similar from Muqatil and from Ibn 'Abbas. He mentioned from 'Ali ibn al-Husayn that Allah revealed to His Prophet ﷺ that Zayd would divorce Zaynab and that Allah would marry her to His Messenger ﷺ; and after he knew this through revelation, he said to Zayd: ﴿Keep your wife to yourself﴾. And what he concealed within himself was that Allah would marry her to him, may Allah be pleased with her. Then al-Qurtubi said, after mentioning this view: Our scholars, may Allah's mercy be upon them, said: This view is the best that has been said concerning the interpretation of this verse, and it is what the people of verification among the exegetes and the firmly grounded scholars hold, such as al-Zuhri, the judge Bakr ibn al-'Ala' al-Qushayri, the judge Abu Bakr ibn al-'Arabi, and others. He continued: As for what is reported that the Prophet ﷺ was fond of Zaynab, the wife of Zayd, and some frivolous people have sometimes used the word "passionate love," this only comes from one who is ignorant of the infallibility of the Prophet ﷺ regarding such matters, or one who makes light of his sanctity.

Al-Tirmidhi al-Hakim, in Nawadir al-Usul, attributed to 'Ali ibn al-Husayn the saying: 'Ali ibn al-Husayn brought this from the treasury of knowledge, a jewel among jewels and a pearl among pearls, that Allah only rebuked him for the fact that He had informed him that she would be one of his wives. How then could he say to Zayd afterward: ﴿Keep your wife to yourself﴾, and the fear of people's talk took hold of you, that they would say: he married his son's wife, while Allah has more right that you fear Him? The purpose of his words ends here.

Ibn Kathir, may Allah have mercy on him, said in his tafsir of this verse: Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Jarir mentioned here reports from some of the early Muslims, may Allah be pleased with them. We prefer to set them aside entirely because they are not sound, so we will not cite them (p-241) up to the end of his words. In it is the statement of 'Ali ibn al-Husayn that we mentioned a little earlier.

The one who wrote these notes, may Allah forgive him and pardon him, says: The verified view in this matter, if Allah wills, is what we mentioned, that the Qur'an indicates it: Allah informed His Prophet ﷺ that Zayd would divorce Zaynab and that He would marry her to him ﷺ, while at that time she was under Zayd's wedlock. When Zayd complained of her to him ﷺ, he said to him: ﴿Keep your wife to yourself and fear Allah﴾. So Allah rebuked him for his saying: ﴿Keep your wife to yourself﴾, after he knew that she would become his own wife ﷺ, and he feared the people's talk, that they would say: If he had made known what he knew of his marrying her, that he wanted to marry his son's wife at the time when she was in Zayd's wedlock.

The evidence for this is two matters:

The first: what we have already mentioned, that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿And you were concealing within yourself that which Allah was to bring to light﴾. What Allah, Mighty and Majestic, brought to light is his marriage to her, in His saying: ﴿So when Zayd had no longer any need for her, We married her to you﴾. Allah, Mighty and Majestic, did not bring to light anything of what they alleged, that he loved her. Had that been the intended meaning, Allah would have brought it to light, as you see.

The second matter: Allah, Mighty and Majestic, explicitly stated that it was He who married her to him, and that the divine wisdom in that marriage was to abolish the prohibition on the wives of adopted sons, in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So when Zayd had no longer any need for her, We married her to you, so that there would be no difficulty for the believers concerning the wives of their adopted sons﴾, to the end of the verse. His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿so that there would be no difficulty for the believers﴾, is an explicit explanation (ta'lil) of his marrying her for the reason we mentioned. That Allah is the One who married her to him for this great wisdom is explicit that the cause of his marrying her was not his love for her, which had been the cause of Zayd's divorcing her, as they claimed. This is made clear by His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So when Zayd had no longer any need for her﴾ up to the end of the verse, because it indicates that Zayd had fulfilled his need from her, and he no longer had any desire for her, so he divorced her by his own choice. And Allah knows best.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 33, verse 41:

The Almighty's statement: ﴿O you who have believed, remember Allah with much remembrance.﴾

What this noble verse includes of the command to increase in remembrance of Allah has its meaning in other verses, such as:

• His statement, the Exalted: ﴿So remember Allah while standing, sitting, and [lying] on your sides﴾ [an-Nisa: 103],

• and His statement, the Exalted: ﴿Those who remember Allah while standing, sitting, and on their sides﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 191],

• and His statement, the Exalted: ﴿And the men who remember Allah much and the women who remember [Him]﴾ and the verse [al-Ahzab: 35],

and other verses besides these.

(p-242) His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And give good tidings to the believers that they will have from Allah a great bounty﴾. Here He did not specify what is meant by the "great bounty" in this noble verse, but He explained it in Surah ash-Shura in His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And those who believe and do righteous deeds, [they will be] in the meadows of the gardens; for them is whatever they wish with their Lord. That is the great bounty﴾ [ash-Shura: 22].

The author said in *Daf' Iham al-Idtirab 'an Ayat al-Kitab*:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿O Prophet, indeed We have made lawful for you your wives…﴾ [the verse].

It appears to contradict His saying: ﴿Women are not lawful for you after this…﴾ [al-Ahzab: 52].

The answer is that His saying ﴿Women are not lawful for you﴾ is abrogated (mansukh) by His saying ﴿Indeed, We have made lawful for you your wives﴾. We have already mentioned in Surat al-Baqarah that this is one of the two places in the Mushaf where the abrogating verse comes before the abrogated one, because of its earlier position in the arrangement of the Mushaf, even though it was revealed later, according to the view held on this matter.

It was also said that the abrogating verse is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿You may defer whom you wish of them﴾ [the verse] [al-Ahzab: 51].

Some scholars said that the verse is muhkam (not abrogated). According to this view, the meaning is: ﴿Women are not lawful for you after this﴾, that is, after the women whom Allah made lawful for you in His saying ﴿Indeed, We have made lawful for you your wives﴾ [the verse].

Thus the verse ﴿Women are not lawful for you﴾ prohibits whoever has not been included in the verse ﴿Indeed, We have made lawful for you your wives﴾, such as the women of the People of the Book, the polytheist women, and the Bedouin women, according to the view that this applies to them, as well as the daughters of paternal uncles and paternal aunts, and the daughters of maternal uncles and maternal aunts who did not migrate with him, according to the view that this also applies to them.

The view that there is no abrogation was held by Ubayy ibn Ka'b, Mujahid in one narration from him, Ikrimah, al-Dahhak in one narration, Abu Razin in one narration from him, Abu Salih, al-Hasan, Qatadah in one narration, al-Suddi, and others, as Ibn Kathir and others transmitted from them. Ibn Jarir and Abu Hayyan chose the view of no abrogation.

What appears to us is that the view of abrogation is stronger. What makes us prefer it is not that it is the view of a group of the Companions and those after them, among them Ali, Ibn Abbas, Anas, and others, but what makes us prefer it is that it is the view of the people most knowledgeable about the matter, namely his wives (ﷺ), because no one is more concerned with the question of whether other co-wives are lawful or not than they are. They are the companions of the story (sawahibat al-qissah).

It has been established in the science of usul (principles of jurisprudence) that the person who is the subject of the story takes precedence over others. For this reason, scholars preferred the report of Maymunah and Abu Rafi' that he (ﷺ) married her while he was not in the state of ihram, over the report of Ibn Abbas, on which there is agreement, that he married her while in ihram, because Maymunah was the one concerned in the story and Abu Rafi' was the intermediary in it.

Having known this, you should know that among those who held the view of abrogation was the Mother of the Believers 'A'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her, who said: "He (ﷺ) did not die until Allah made women lawful for him." The Mother of the Believers Umm Salamah, may Allah be pleased with her, said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) did not die until Allah made lawful for him to marry from among women whomever he wished, except one who is a close relative (dhat mahram)."

As for 'A'ishah, this was narrated from her by Imam Ahmad, al-Tirmidhi who graded it sahih, al-Nasa'i in his Sunan, al-Hakim who graded it sahih, Abu Dawud in his book on abrogation (Nasikh), Ibn al-Mundhir, and others.

(p-371) As for Umm Salamah, this was narrated from her by Ibn Abi Hatim, as Ibn Kathir and others transmitted from him. What supports this is what a group narrated from Abdullah ibn Shaddad, may Allah be pleased with him, that "the Prophet (ﷺ) married Umm Habibah and Juwayriyah, may Allah be pleased with them both, after the revelation of: ﴿Women are not lawful for you﴾."

Al-Alusi said in his tafsir: "This was narrated from him by Ibn Abi Shaybah, Abd ibn Humayd, and Ibn Abi Hatim." And Allah knows best.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 33, verse 53 (part 1 of 4):

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when you ask them for something, ask them from behind a screen. That is purer for your hearts and their hearts.﴾

We have already mentioned, in the introduction to this blessed book, that among the kinds of clarification (bayan) it contains is that some scholars state an opinion regarding a verse, while within the same verse there is an indication (qarinah) showing that this opinion is not correct. We gave examples of this in the introduction, and many more examples in the book that were not mentioned in the introduction. Among the examples we mentioned in the introduction is this noble verse. We said in the introduction to this blessed book that many people say the verse of the "hijab," namely His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when you ask them for something, ask them from behind a screen,﴾ is specific to the wives of the Prophet ﷺ. His exalted statement giving the reason for this ruling, which is the obligation of the screen, namely that it is purer for the hearts of men and women from doubt, in His saying: ﴿That is purer for your hearts and their hearts,﴾ is a clear indication that the ruling is intended to be general, since none of all the Muslims has said that other than the wives of the Prophet ﷺ have no need for the purity of their hearts and the hearts of men from suspicion regarding them. It is established in the principles of jurisprudence (usul) that the cause ('illah) may generalize its effect (ma'lul), and the poet of Maraqi al-Su'ud pointed to this with his saying:

"It may specify and it may generalize its root, but it does not undermine it."

The point of our statement in the aforementioned introduction ends here.

From what we have mentioned, you know that in this noble verse there is clear evidence that the obligation of the hijab is a general ruling for all women, not specific to his wives ﷺ, even though the original wording is specific to them; because the generality of its cause is evidence of the generality of the ruling concerning it. The method of the cause (maslak al-'illah) that shows that His saying: ﴿That is purer for your hearts and their hearts﴾ is the cause of His saying: ﴿ask them from behind a screen,﴾ is the method known in the principles of jurisprudence as the method of allusion and indication (maslak al-ima' wa'l-tanbih). The governing rule of this method, which applies to its particulars, is that a descriptive attribute (wasf) is attached to a legal ruling in such a way that, if that attribute were not the cause of that ruling, the speech would be faulty in the eyes of those who understand. The author of Maraqi al-Su'ud defined the indication and alerting (dalalat al-ima' wa'l-tanbih) in the discussion of the implication of necessity, allusion, indication and alerting (dalalat al-iqtida' wa'l-isharah wa'l-ima' wa'l-tanbih) with his saying:

"The implication of allusion and alerting, in the art, is what its practitioners intend:
that an attribute be joined to a ruling, if it is not for a cause, the discerning one will find it faulty."

He also defined allusion and alerting among the paths of the 'illah with his saying: "The third is allusion: the joining of the attribute with the ruling, both expressed, without contradiction.
That attribute, or its equivalent, its joining to other than it would be harmful."

So His saying, exalted is He: ﴿That is purer for your hearts and their hearts,﴾ if it were not the cause of His saying: ﴿ask them from behind a screen,﴾ the speech would be faulty and disordered in the eyes of the discerning, knowledgeable person.

When you know that His saying, exalted is He: ﴿That is purer for your hearts and their hearts﴾ is the cause of His saying: ﴿ask them from behind a screen,﴾ and you know that the ruling of the cause is general, then know that the cause may generalize its effect, and it may specify it, as we mentioned in the verse of the Maraqi al-Su'ud, and by this you know that the ruling of the verse of the hijab is general because its cause is general. And since the ruling of this verse is general by the indication of the Qur'anic qarinah,

know that the hijab is obligatory for all women by the indication of the Qur'an.

Know that in this discussion we intend to mention the Qur'anic evidences for the obligation of the hijab in general, then the evidences from the Sunnah, then we discuss the evidences of both sides, and mention the answer to the evidences of those who said that the hijab is not obligatory for women other than his wives ﷺ. We have already mentioned that His saying: ﴿That is purer for your hearts﴾ is an indication of the generality of the ruling of the verse of the hijab.

Among the Qur'anic evidences for the veiling of the woman and her covering of her entire body, even her face, is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O Prophet, tell your wives and your daughters and the women of the believers to draw their outer garments over themselves.﴾ [al-Ahzab: 59]. Many people of knowledge have said that the meaning of ﴿draw their outer garments over themselves﴾ is that they cover all their faces with them, so that nothing appears of them except one eye with which they see. Among those who said this are Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Abbas, 'Abidah al-Salmani and others.

(p-244) If it is said: The wording of the noble verse, namely His saying: ﴿draw over themselves from their outer garments,﴾ does not linguistically entail covering the face, and no text from the Book, the Sunnah, or consensus has established that it entails that. The statement of some exegetes that it entails it is countered by the statement of others that it does not entail it, and with this the argument from the verse for the obligation of covering the face falls away.

The answer: In the noble verse there is a clear qarinah that His saying in it: ﴿draw over themselves from their outer garments﴾ includes in its meaning the covering of their faces by drawing their outer garments over them. The qarinah mentioned is His saying: ﴿Say to your wives,﴾ and the obligation for his wives to veil and cover their faces is not disputed among the Muslims. So mentioning the wives alongside the daughters and the women of the believers indicates the obligation of covering the faces by drawing the outer garments, as you see.

Among the other evidences for this is what we previously mentioned in Surah al-Nur, in discussing His saying: ﴿and not to reveal their adornment except what appears of it﴾ [al-Ghafir: 31], that the inductive survey of the Qur'an shows that the meaning of ﴿except what appears of it﴾ is the outer wrap over the garments, and that it is not valid to interpret ﴿except what appears of it﴾ as the face and the two hands, as has been previously clarified.

Know that the saying of one who said: there is a Qur'anic qarinah that His saying: ﴿draw over themselves from their outer garments﴾ does not include covering the face, and that the qarinah mentioned is His saying: ﴿That is more suitable that they be recognized,﴾ and he said: His saying, "that they be recognized," indicates that they are unveiled, uncovering their faces, because the one whose face is covered is not recognized, is false, and its falsity is clear, and the context of the verse prohibits it absolutely; because His saying: ﴿draw over themselves from their outer garments﴾ is explicit in forbidding that.

Its clarification: the reference in His saying: ﴿That is more suitable that they be recognized﴾ returns to their drawing their outer garments over themselves, and their drawing their outer garments over themselves cannot in any way be "more suitable that they be recognized" by unveiling and uncovering their faces, as you see. The drawing of the outer garments contradicts recognition being personal recognition through uncovering the faces, as is not hidden.

His saying in the noble verse: "to your wives" is also evidence that the recognition mentioned in the verse is not by uncovering the faces, because their veiling is not disputed among the Muslims.

The summary: the said statement is refuted by several proofs:

(p-245) The first: the context of the verse, as we clarified above.

The second: His saying, "to your wives," as we also clarified.

The third: that the majority of exegetes from the Companions and those after them explained the verse while stating its occasion of revelation: that the women of Madinah used to go out at night to relieve themselves outside the houses, and some of the wicked men in Madinah would approach the slave women but not the free women. Some of the women of the believers went out in a dress not distinguished from the dress of slave women, so those wicked men would harass them, thinking that they were slave women. So God commanded His Prophet ﷺ to order his wives, his daughters and the women of the believers to distinguish themselves in their dress from the dress of slave women, by drawing their outer garments over themselves. When they did that and the wicked men saw them, they knew that they were free women, and their knowledge that they are free and not slaves is the meaning of His saying: ﴿That is more suitable that they be recognized,﴾ so it is recognition by the attribute, not by the person. This explanation is consistent with the apparent meaning of the Qur'an, as you see.

So His saying: ﴿draw over themselves from their outer garments,﴾ because their drawing it over themselves indicates that they are free women, so it is more suitable and closer to their being recognized, that is, it is known that they are free women, so they are not harmed by the wicked men who approach slave women. This is what the people of knowledge of exegesis explained this verse with, and it is clear. It does not mean that the approach of the wicked men to slave women is permissible; it is forbidden, and there is no doubt that those who approach them are among "those in whose hearts is a disease," and that they enter into the generality of His saying: ﴿and those in whose hearts is a disease﴾ [al-Ahzab: 60], in His saying: ﴿and those in whose hearts is a disease,﴾ up to His saying: ﴿and they will be killed, a [thorough] killing.﴾ [al-Ahzab: 60-61].

Among what indicates that one who approaches what is not lawful of women is among those in whose hearts is a disease is His saying: ﴿So do not be soft in speech, lest one in whose heart is a disease should covet﴾ up to the verse [al-Ahzab: 32]. That is a known meaning in the speech of the Arabs, and from it is the saying of al-A'sha:

"Guarding of the chastity, content with piety,
not of those whose heart in it is diseased."

In summary: there is no difficulty regarding free women opposing the dress of slave women so that the wicked men will respect them, and averting the harm of the wicked men from slave women is necessary, and it has other causes, not including drawing the outer garments.

* *

Note.

We have previously mentioned in Surah Bani Isra'il, in discussing His saying: ﴿Indeed, this Qur'an guides to that which is most suitable,﴾ (p-246) that the verbal form (al-fi'l al-sina'i) according to the grammarians dissolves into a verbal noun (masdar) and a tense; as Ibn Malik said in the Khulasah:

"The verbal noun is the name of what is other than the time among the connotations of the verb, like 'amn from amina."

And that according to groups of the rhetoricians it dissolves into a verbal noun, a tense and an attribution.

Knowing this, know that the verbal noun and the tense are both latent in the concept of the verb by consensus, and references and pronouns may sometimes return to the verbal noun latent in the concept of the verb, and sometimes to the tense latent in it.

An example of a demonstrative returning to the latent verbal noun is His saying here: ﴿They draw over themselves,﴾ then He said: ﴿That is more suitable that they be recognized,﴾ meaning: that drawing over, understood from His saying "they draw over."

An example of a demonstrative returning to the latent tense is His saying: ﴿And the Horn is blown; that is the Day of the Threat﴾ [Qaf: 20], so His saying "that" means the time of blowing understood from His saying "and was blown," meaning: that time is the Day of the Threat.

Among the evidences that the ruling of the verse of the hijab is general is what is established in the principles of jurisprudence, that the address to one person's ruling encompasses the whole Ummah, and the ruling is not specific to that one addressed. We have clarified this issue in Surah al-Hajj, in the discussion of the prohibition of wearing saffron-dyed clothing, and we said in that: the address of the Prophet ﷺ to one of his Ummah encompasses the ruling for the whole Ummah, because they are equal in the rulings of obligation, unless there is a specific evidence that must be referred to. The disagreement of the scholars of usul regarding the address to one person, whether it is one of the forms of generality indicating the generality of the ruling, is a disagreement in terminology, not a real disagreement. The address to one person according to the Hanbalis is a form of generality, and according to others among the Malikis, Shafi'is and others, the address to one person does not generalize, because the wording for one person does not by convention include others, and if it does not include him by convention, it is not a form of generality. But the people of this view agree that the ruling of the address to one person is general to others, but by another evidence other than the address to one person, and that evidence is by the text and by analogy.

As for analogy, it is evident, because analogizing other than that addressed upon him, by the common ground of the equality of the addressees in the rulings of obligation, is a clear analogy.

As for the text, it is like his saying ﷺ in the pledge of allegiance of women: "I do not shake hands with women, and my word to one woman is only like my word to a hundred women." (p-247)

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 33, verse 53 (part 2 of 4):

They say: among the evidences for this is the hadith: "My ruling on the one is my ruling on the group." Ibn Qasim al-'Abbadi said in al-Ayat al-Bayyinat: Know that the hadith "My ruling on the one is my ruling on the group" is not known to have a source with this wording. However, al-Tirmidhi narrated it and said: hasan sahih. And al-Nasa'i, Ibn Majah and Ibn Hibban (narrated) his saying (ﷺ) concerning the pledge of allegiance of women: "Indeed I do not shake hands with women," and he cited the hadith as we have mentioned it. The author of Kashf al-Khafa' wa Muzil al-Ilbas 'amma ishtahara min al-ahadith 'ala alsinat al-nas said: "My ruling on the one is my ruling on the group," and in one wording: "like my ruling on the group," has no source with this wording, as al-'Iraqi said in his takhrij of the hadiths of al-Baydawi. He said in al-Durar, like al-Zarkashi: it is not known. Al-Mizzi and al-Dhahabi were asked about it and they denied it. Yes, what supports it is what al-Tirmidhi and al-Nasa'i narrated from the hadith of Umayma bint Ruqayqa. The wording of al-Nasa'i is: "My saying to one woman is only like my saying to a hundred women," and the wording of al-Tirmidhi is: "My saying to a hundred women is only like my saying to one woman." This is among the hadiths which al-Daraqutni obliged the two Shaykhs (al-Bukhari and Muslim) to include, because it is authentic according to their condition. Ibn Qasim al-'Abbadi said in Sharh al-Waraqat al-Kabir: "My ruling on the one" is not known to have a source, to its end, close to what we have quoted from him. End.

The one who annotates it, may Allah pardon him and forgive him, says: The hadith mentioned is authentic from the hadith of Umayma bint Ruqayqa, spelled with two qaf's, diminutive. She is a Companion among those who pledged allegiance. Ruqayqa is her mother, and she is the sister of Khadija bint Khuwaylid; it was said she was her paternal aunt. Her father's name is Bijad (with a b, then a j), son of 'Abd Allah ibn 'Umayr al-Taymi, of Taym ibn Murra. He alluded to this in Maraqi al-Su'ud with his saying:
"One address is for other than the Hanbali, without regard to the text and the clear analogy."
End of the relevant point from it.

* *

By this usuli principle which we have mentioned, you know that the ruling of the verse of hijab is general, even though its wording is specific to his wives (ﷺ); because his saying to one woman, whether of his wives or of others, is like his saying to a hundred women, as you have seen its clarification shortly before.

Among the Qur'anic evidences that indicate hijab is the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And as for women past child-bearing who have no hope of marriage, there is no blame upon them for putting aside their outer garments without displaying adornment. But to refrain is better for them. And Allah is Hearing and Knowing.﴾ [al-Nur: 60] (p-248) Because Allah, Mighty and Majestic, explained in this noble verse that al-qawa'id, i.e., the elderly women who have no hope of marriage, meaning they do not aspire to marriage due to old age and men's lack of need for them, are granted a concession, lifting blame from them for laying aside their garments, on condition that they do not display adornment. Then He, Mighty and Majestic, despite all this, said: ﴿but to refrain is better for them﴾, i.e., refraining from laying aside garments is better for them; that is, their refraining from laying aside their garments despite their old age and the cutting off of their hope of marriage, and their not displaying adornment, is better for them.

The most apparent of the opinions regarding His saying: ﴿lay aside their garments﴾ is that it means laying aside what is above the khimar and the shirt, of the outer cloaks (jalabib) which are over the khimar and the garments.

So the saying of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, in this noble verse: ﴿but to refrain is better for them﴾ is a clear proof that a woman who has beauty and has desire for marriage is not granted a concession to lay aside any of her garments, nor to neglect any part of covering in the presence of non-mahram men.

And when you know from what we have mentioned that the ruling of the verse of hijab is general, and that what we have mentioned along with it of verses contains the indication of covering the whole body of the woman from non-mahram men, you know that the Qur'an indicates hijab. Even if we assume that the verse of hijab is specific to his wives (ﷺ), there is no doubt that they are the best example for the women of the Muslims in noble manners that require complete purity and freedom from the filth of suspicion. Whoever today tries to prevent the women of the Muslims, such as the advocates of unveiling, display and mixing, from emulating them in this heavenly noble etiquette, which includes the safety of honour and purity from the stain of suspicion, is a deceiver to the nation of Muhammad (ﷺ) and sick at heart, as you see.

Know that alongside the Qur'an's indication of the woman's covering from non-mahram men, prophetic hadiths also indicate it. Among them is what al-Shaykhan (al-Bukhari and Muslim) recorded in their Sahihs and others, from the hadith of 'Uqba ibn 'Amir al-Juhani, may Allah be pleased with him: that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Beware of entering upon women." A man from the Ansar said: O Messenger of Allah, what about the hamw (the husband's relatives)? He said: "The hamw is death." Al-Bukhari recorded this hadith in the Book of Marriage, in the chapter: "No man should be alone with a woman unless she has a mahram," etc. Muslim recorded it in the Book of Salam, in the chapter on the prohibition of seclusion with a non-mahram woman and entering upon her. So this sound hadith, in which the Prophet (ﷺ) explicitly warned sternly against entering upon women, is a clear proof of the prohibition of entering upon them and asking them for something except from behind a screen (p-249) hijab; because whoever asks her for something not from behind a screen has entered upon her, and the Prophet (ﷺ) warned against entering upon her. When the Ansari asked him about the hamw, who is the husband's relative who is not a mahram to his wife, such as his brother, his nephew, his paternal uncle, his paternal cousin and the like, he (ﷺ) said: "The hamw is death." He (ﷺ) called the entry of a man's relative upon his wife, when he is not a mahram to her, by the name of death. There is no doubt that this expression is the most eloquent of warnings, because death is the most dreadful event that befalls a person in this world, as the poet said:
"Death is the greatest calamity that passes over the creation (jibilla)."
Jibilla means creation, and from it is His saying: ﴿And fear He who created you and the generations before you﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 184]. So his (ﷺ) strong warning against men entering upon women, and his expression of a relative's entry upon his relative's wife by the name of death, is a sound prophetic proof that His saying: ﴿ask them from behind a screen﴾ is general to all women, as you see. For if its ruling were specific to his wives (ﷺ), he would not have issued such a severe general warning to men against entering upon women. The apparent meaning of the hadith is a warning against entering upon them even if no seclusion occurs between them, and that is so; entering upon them and being alone with them are both forbidden with a severe prohibition each on its own, as we previously mentioned that Muslim, may Allah have mercy on him, recorded this hadith in the chapter on the prohibition of seclusion with a non-mahram woman and entering upon her, which indicates that both are forbidden.

Ibn Hajar said in Fath al-Bari, in explaining the hadith mentioned: "Iyyakum wa al-dukhul" (Beware of entering), in the accusative on the basis of warning, which is alerting the addressee to a danger so that he may guard against it; as is said: "Iyyaka wa al-asad" (Beware of you and the lion). His saying "iyyakum" is an object of a hidden verb whose estimate is: "ittaqu" (fear/guard against).

The sense of the sentence is: guard yourselves against entering upon women, and women against entering upon you. In the narration of Ibn Wahb, the wording is: "Do not enter upon women," and the prohibition of entering includes the prohibition of seclusion with them, a fortiori. End of the relevant point from it.

Al-Bukhari, may Allah have mercy on him, said in his Sahih, chapter: ﴿And let them draw their khimars over their bosoms﴾. Ahmad ibn Shabib said: My father narrated to us from Yunus, who said: Ibn Shihab said, from 'Urwa, from 'A'isha, may Allah be pleased with her, who said: May Allah have mercy on the first emigrant women. When Allah revealed: ﴿And let them draw their khimars over their bosoms﴾ [al-Nur: 31], they tore their murut (cloaks) and covered themselves with them.

Abu Nu'aym narrated to us: Ibrahim ibn Nafi' narrated to us, from al-Hasan ibn Muslim, from Safiyya bint Shayba: (p-250) that 'A'isha, may Allah be pleased with her, used to say: When this verse was revealed: ﴿And let them draw their khimars over their bosoms﴾, they took their izars and tore them at the edges, and covered themselves with them. End from Sahih al-Bukhari.

Ibn Hajar said in al-Fath, in explaining this hadith: "Fakhtamarna" means they covered their faces. The manner of that is that she places the khimar on her head and throws it from the right side over the left shoulder; this is taqannu' (veiling). Al-Farra' said: In the pre-Islamic era, a woman would let her khimar down behind her and uncover what was in front of her, so they were commanded to conceal themselves. End of the relevant point from Fath al-Bari.

This sound hadith is explicit that the Companion women mentioned in it understood that the meaning of His saying: ﴿And let them draw their khimars over their bosoms﴾ requires covering their faces, and that they tore their izars and covered themselves, i.e., covered their faces with them, in compliance with Allah's command in His saying: ﴿And let them draw their khimars over their bosoms﴾, which requires covering their faces. By this, the fair-minded person realises that the covering of the woman from men and her covering of her face from them is established in the sound Sunnah which explains the Book of Allah, the Exalted. 'A'isha, may Allah be pleased with her, praised those women for their hastening to obey Allah's commands in His Book. It is known that they did not understand the covering of the faces from His saying: ﴿And let them draw their khimars over their bosoms﴾ except from the Prophet (ﷺ), because he was alive and they would ask him about everything that was unclear to them in their religion, and Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿And We have sent down to you the Reminder, that you may make clear to the people what has been sent down to them﴾ [al-Nahl: 44]. So it is not possible that they explained it on their own accord. Ibn Hajar said in Fath al-Bari: Ibn Abi Hatim has, through 'Abd Allah ibn 'Uthman ibn Khuthaym, from Safiyya, something that clarifies this, and its wording is: We mentioned to 'A'isha the women of Quraysh and their virtue. She said: Indeed the women of Quraysh have virtue, but by Allah, I have not seen better women than the women of the Ansar, more firm in belief in the Book of Allah, nor more faithful to the revelation. When the Surah "al-Nur" was revealed: ﴿And let them draw their khimars over their bosoms﴾, their men returned to them reciting to them what had been revealed concerning it, and not one of them remained but she went to her murut and wrapped herself in it, so they prayed the dawn prayer covered (mu'taj'irat), as if crows were upon their heads. End of the relevant point from Fath al-Bari.

The meaning of mu'tajirat is mukhtamirat (covered with khimars), as clarified in the narration of al-Bukhari mentioned just above. So 'A'isha, may Allah be pleased with her, despite her knowledge, understanding and piety, praised them with this great praise, and declared that she had not seen any more firm than them in belief in the Book of Allah or in faith in the revelation. This is a clear proof that their understanding of the obligation to cover the faces from His saying: ﴿And let them draw their khimars over their bosoms﴾ was part of their belief in the Book of Allah and their faith in its revelation, and it is explicit that women's seclusion from men and their covering of their faces is a belief in the Book of Allah and faith in its revelation, as you see. (p-251) How utterly strange it is that someone among those who claim to be scholars asserts that nothing in the Book or the Sunnah indicates a woman's covering of her face from non-mahram men, when the Companion women did so, obeying Allah's command in His Book out of faith in its revelation; and the meaning of this is established in the Sahih, as passed from al-Bukhari. This is among the greatest and clearest evidences for the obligation of hijab upon all the women of the Muslims, as you see.

Ibn Kathir, may Allah have mercy on him, said in his tafsir: Al-Bazzar also said: Muhammad ibn al-Muthanna narrated to us, Amr ibn Asim narrated to me, Hammam narrated to us, from Qatada, from Muwarriq, from Abu al-Ahwas, from Abdullah (may Allah be pleased with him), from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "Indeed the woman is 'awrah (a part to be concealed). When she goes out, Satan looks at her with desire (istashrafaha). She is nearest to her Lord's mercy (rawhah) when she is in the innermost part of her house." Al-Tirmidhi narrated it from Bundar, from Amr ibn Asim, with the same meaning. End of quotation from him.

The author of Majma' al-Zawa'id (al-Haythami) also mentioned this hadith and said: Al-Tabarani narrated it in al-Kabir, and its narrators are trustworthy (muwaththaqun). This hadith supports all the evidences we have mentioned. Its statement that the woman is 'awrah indicates the obligation of hijab (veiling), because it is necessary to cover everything to which the term 'awrah applies.

Among what supports this is what al-Haythami also mentioned in Majma' al-Zawa'id, from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: "Women are only 'awrah. A woman goes out from her house when there is no harm in her, and Satan looks at her with desire, and says: 'You do not pass by anyone without pleasing him.' A woman dresses herself, and he says to her: 'Where are you going?' She says: 'I am visiting a sick person, or attending a funeral, or praying in a mosque.' No woman worships her Lord like the worship she performs in her house." Then he said: Al-Tabarani narrated it in al-Kabir, and its narrators are reliable (thiqat). End of quotation from him. A statement like this has the ruling of a marfu' (attributed to the Prophet), since there is no room for personal opinion (ra'y) in it.

Among the evidences indicating this are the hadiths we presented earlier, which show that a woman's prayer in her house is better for her than her prayer in the mosques. We explained this in Surah al-Nur, in discussing His saying: ﴿Men who glorify Him therein morning and evening﴾ [al-Nur: 36-37]. Hadiths of this kind are very numerous, and what we have mentioned is sufficient for one who seeks the truth.

We have mentioned the Qur'anic verses that indicate this, and the authentic (sahih) hadiths that indicate hijab. We have shown that among the clearest of them in this matter is the verse of al-Nur, together with the tafsir of the Companions (sahabah) of it, which is His saying: ﴿And let them draw their veils over their bosoms﴾. We have explained, not long ago, the Companions' tafsir of it, while the Prophet (ﷺ) was present among them and revelation was descending upon him, that its intended meaning includes covering the face and veiling it from men, and that a woman's covering of her face is an act in accordance with the Qur'an, as 'A'ishah (may Allah be pleased with her) said.

Since you know that this amount of evidence for the general obligation of hijab is enough for the fair-minded, we will now mention for you the answers of the scholars to what was used as evidence by those who said that it is permissible for a woman to show her face and hands in the presence of non-mahram men.

Among the hadiths they used as evidence for this is the hadith of Khalid ibn Duraik, from 'A'ishah (may Allah be pleased with her): that Asma' bint Abi Bakr entered upon the Prophet (ﷺ) wearing thin garments, so he turned away from her and said: "O Asma', when a woman reaches menstruation, it is not proper that anything of her be seen except this," and he pointed to his face and his palms. This hadith is answered by saying that it is weak from two aspects:

The first: It is mursal (a hadith whose chain skips a Companion), because Khalid ibn Duraik did not hear from 'A'ishah, as Abu Dawud and Abu Hatim al-Razi said, as we mentioned earlier in Surah al-Nur.

The second aspect: In its chain (isnad) is Sa'id ibn Bashir al-Azdi, their mawla (client). About him, in al-Taqrib, it is said: "weak." Moreover, it is rejected by the evidences we have mentioned for the general obligation of hijab. And even if its authenticity were assumed, it may be interpreted as having occurred before the command of hijab.

Among the hadiths they used as evidence for this is the hadith of Jabir, which is established in the Sahih: He said: "I witnessed with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) the prayer on the day of 'Eid. He began with the prayer before the khutbah (sermon), without adhan or iqamah. Then he stood leaning on Bilal, and he commanded the people to fear Allah, urged them to obey Him, admonished the people and reminded them. Then he proceeded until he reached the women, and he admonished them and reminded them, and said: 'Give charity, for most of you are fuel for Hell.' Then a woman from among the women of standing (sifah) rose, with two dark marks on her cheeks (saf'a' al-khaddayn), and said: 'Why, O Messenger of Allah?' He said: 'Because you complain excessively and are ungrateful to your husbands (ta-kfurna al-ashir).' He said: So they began to give charity from their jewelry, throwing into Bilal's garment their earrings and their rings." End of quotation. This is the wording of Muslim in his Sahih.

They said: Jabir's statement in this hadith, "saf'a' al-khaddayn," indicates that she was uncovering her face, because if she had been veiled, he would not have seen her cheeks, nor would he have known that she had marks on her cheeks.

It is answered regarding this hadith of Jabir: There is nothing in it that indicates that the Prophet (ﷺ) saw her uncovering her face and approved of that. Rather, the most that the hadith conveys is that Jabir saw her face. That does not necessarily imply that she uncovered it intentionally. Many a woman's veil slips from her face without intent, so some people see it in that state, as Nabigha Dhubyani said:

"The veil (nasif) fell, and she did not intend its falling, so she caught it, and protected herself from us with her hand."

So the one who argues from the hadith of Jabir mentioned above must establish that the Prophet (ﷺ) saw her unveiled and approved of that, and he has no way to establish this. Other than Jabir also narrated this story, and none of them mentioned the uncovering of that woman's face. Muslim, in his Sahih, mentioned among those who narrated it other than Jabir: Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, Ibn 'Abbas, and Ibn 'Umar. Others mentioned it from others. None of those who narrated the story other than Jabir said that he saw the cheeks of that woman with the marks on her cheeks. With this you know that there is no evidence for unveiling (sufur) in the hadith of Jabir mentioned.

Al-Nawawi said, in his commentary on this hadith of Jabir in Muslim, regarding the statement "a woman from among the women of standing (min sitat al-nisa')": this is how it is in the copies, sitah with a kasrah on the sin and a fathah on the light taa'. In some copies it is wasitat al-nisa'. Al-Qadi said: Its meaning is "from their best," and wasat means justice and excellence. He said: Our skilled shaykhs claimed that this word is altered in Muslim's book, and that its correct form is "from the lowest of the women (siflat al-nisa')." Likewise Ibn Abi Shaybah narrated it in his Musnad, and al-Nasa'i in his Sunan. In a narration of Ibn Abi Shaybah: "a woman who is not of the elite of women." This is the opposite of the first interpretation, and it is supported by his statement after it: "saf'a' al-khaddayn." End of al-Qadi's words.

This claim of altering the word is not acceptable. Rather, the word is correct, and the intended meaning is not "from the best of women" as he explained it. Rather, the intended meaning is: a woman from the middle of the women, sitting in the middle of them. Al-Jawhari and others from the people of language said: It is said wasatu al-qawm, asitu-hum, wasutan, wasitatan, meaning: I came into the middle of them. End of his words.

This last interpretation is the correct one. There is absolutely no praise in the hadith of Jabir for the aforementioned woman with the marks on her cheeks. It is possible that Jabir mentioned the marks on her cheeks to indicate that she was not one whom men would be attracted to, because marks on the cheeks are an ugliness in women. Al-Nawawi said: "saf'a' al-khaddayn" means there is a change and blackness in them. Al-Jawhari said in his Sihah: "al-saf'ah" in the face is blackness on the cheeks of a pale woman. The dove is called "saf'a'" because of the mark on its neck. Humayd ibn Thawr said:

"Of the pigeons, one with a mark on both sides of her neck came early, to the tops of tamarisk trees at sunrise, blackened."

The one who compiles this, may Allah pardon him and forgive him, says: The saf'ah on the cheeks is among the well-known meanings in the language of the Arabs: it is blackness and change in the face, from illness, calamity, or severe travel. From this is the saying of Mutammim ibn Nuwayrah al-Tamimi, mourning his brother Malik:

"The daughter of al-'Umari says, after you have become, I see you dyed, comfortable in mind, noble. I said to her: long grief, when you asked me, and the anguish of longing, which leaves the cheek sallow (asfa')."

It is well known that among the saf'ah there is what is natural, as in falcons. A falcon may have natural blackness on its cheeks. From this is the saying of Zuhayr ibn Abi Sulma:

"He desires her, one with dark cheeks, lowering his head, with the primary feathers of his wings, for whom the nets were not set."

The intended point is that the mark on the cheeks is an indication of the ugliness of the face. Some scholars say that a woman of an ugly face, whom men do not desire because of her ugliness, has the ruling of the qawa'id (women past childbearing) who do not hope for marriage.

Among the hadiths they used as evidence for this is the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas that we mentioned earlier. He said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) took al-Fadl ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with both of them) behind him on his mount on the Day of Sacrifice (yawm al-nahr), and al-Fadl was a handsome man. The Prophet (ﷺ) stopped to give rulings to them, and a woman from Khath'am, beautiful, came asking the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) for a ruling. Al-Fadl began to look at her, and her beauty pleased him. The Prophet (ﷺ) turned, and al-Fadl was looking at her. He turned his hand and took the chin of al-Fadl, and turned his face away from looking at her. She said: 'O Messenger of Allah, the obligation of Allah concerning Hajj upon His servants has reached my father, who is a very old man...'" to the end of the hadith. They said: The report that the Khath'ami woman was beautiful implies that she was uncovering her face.

This is answered in two ways as well:

The first: The answer is that there is nothing in any of the narrations of the hadith that explicitly states that she was uncovering her face, or that the Prophet (ﷺ) saw her uncovering it and approved of that. Rather, the most that the hadith contains is that she was beautiful. In some narrations of the hadith, she is described as "husna' (beautiful)." Knowing that she was beautiful does not necessitate that she was uncovering her face, or that he (ﷺ) approved of that. Rather, her veil may slip from her without intent, so some men see her without intending to uncover her face, as we explained regarding Jabir's seeing the woman with the marks on her cheeks. It is also possible that he knew her beauty before that time, because he may have seen her before and known her.

What makes this clear is that 'Abdullah ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with both of them), from whom this hadith is narrated, was not present at the time of his brother's looking at the woman and her looking at him, because we have mentioned that the Prophet (ﷺ) sent him ahead at night from Muzdalifah to Mina with the weaker members of his family. It is known that he narrated the aforementioned hadith only through his brother al-Fadl, and al-Fadl did not tell him that she was uncovering her face. The awareness of al-Fadl that she was beautiful and attractive does not necessitate unveiling intentionally, because it is possible that he saw her face and recognized its beauty because her veil slipped without intent on her part, and it is possible that he saw her before that and knew her beauty.

If it is said: Her saying "she is beautiful," and his consequent use of the particle "fa" (so) in "al-Fadl began to look at her," and his saying "her beauty pleased him," contain clear evidence that he was seeing her face and looking at it because he was impressed by its beauty.

The answer is: Those indications do not necessarily imply, to the point of exclusion, that she was uncovering her face, and that the Prophet (ﷺ) saw her in that state and approved of it, because of the types of possibility we have mentioned. Moreover, a woman's beauty may be recognized and looked at while she is covered with a head-covering (mukhtamirah), because of the beauty of her figure and her stature. Her grace and beauty may be recognized merely by seeing her fingers, as is well known. For this reason, Ibn Mas'ud interpreted His saying: ﴿And not reveal their adornment except what appears thereof﴾ [al-Nur: 31] as referring to the outer garment over the clothes, as previously mentioned. What makes clear that beauty is recognized beneath clothing is the statement of the poet:

"Umamah circled among the riders at times. How beautiful is her figure, though veiled (muntaqiban)."

He has exaggerated the beauty of her figure, even though it is customary for it to be covered by clothing and not exposed.

The second aspect: the woman is in a state of ihram, and a woman's ihram is in her face and her two palms. So it is obligatory for her to uncover her face if there are no non-related men looking at it, and it is obligatory for her to cover it from men during ihram, as is well known concerning the wives of the Prophet ﷺ and others. No one has said that any man looked at this Khathamiyya woman except al-Fadl ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, and the Prophet ﷺ prevented him from looking at her. By this it is known that she was in ihram, and no one looked at her, so her uncovering her face was then due to her ihram, not to the permissibility of unveiling.

If it is said: her being among the pilgrims makes it likely that men would look at her face if she were unveiled, because most unveiled women in the midst of the pilgrims are not free from men looking at their faces.

The answer: the prevailing character of the Companions of the Prophet ﷺ was scrupulousness and not looking at women. There is no obstacle, rationally, legally or customarily, to the fact that none of them looked at her. Had any of them looked at her, it would have been reported, just as the looking of al-Fadl at her was reported. What is understood from the Prophet ﷺ turning al-Fadl's gaze away from her is that there is no way to leave non-related men looking at a young woman while she is unveiled, as you see, and the preceding evidences have indicated that it is obligatory for her to cover her whole body from them.

In sum, the fair-minded person knows that it is far-fetched in the extreme that the Lawgiver would permit women to uncover the face before non-related men, given that the face is the essence of beauty, and looking at it from a beautiful young woman is the greatest stirrer of human desire and a call to temptation and to falling into what is not proper. Have you not heard some of them say:

Ah, I said: "Allow me to win a single glance,
and let the Resurrection come afterwards."

Are you content, O human, to permit him this glance at your women, your daughters and your sisters? He who said the following spoke the truth:

And it is no wonder that women have become like men,
but the feminization of men is indeed a marvel.

A question related to this noble verse, I mean this verse of the hijab:

Know that it is not permissible for a non-related man to shake hands with a non-related woman.
Nor is it permissible for any part of his body to touch any part of her body.

The evidence for this consists of several matters:

The first: it is established from the Prophet ﷺ that he said: "Indeed I do not shake hands with women," and the hadith continues. And Allah says: ﴿Indeed in the Messenger of Allah you have a good example﴾ [al-Ahzab: 21], so it is incumbent upon us not to shake hands with women, following his example ﷺ. The hadith mentioned is explained in the surah of al-Hajj, in the discussion of the prohibition of men wearing saffron-dyed clothing absolutely, in ihram and otherwise, and in the surah of al-Ahzab, in this verse of the hijab.

That the Prophet ﷺ did not shake hands with women at the time of the pledge is clear evidence that a man does not shake hands with a woman, and no part of his body touches any part of hers, because the lightest type of touching is handshaking. When he ﷺ refrained from it at the time when it would be expected, namely the time of the pledge, this indicates that it is not permissible, and no one has the right to oppose him ﷺ, for he is the one who legislates for his community by his words, his actions and his tacit approval.

The second matter: what we have previously stated, that the woman in her entirety is 'awrah, and it is obligatory for her to veil. The command to lower the gaze was given only out of fear of falling into temptation. There is no doubt that touching of body to body is stronger in stirring desire and stronger in calling to temptation than looking with the eye, and every fair-minded person knows the soundness of this.

The third matter: that this is a means (dhari'a) to enjoying the non-related woman, given the scarcity of fear of Allah in this age, the loss of trustworthiness, and the lack of abstention from doubtful matters. We have been informed repeatedly that some husbands among the common folk kiss their wife's sister by placing the mouth on the mouth, and they call that forbidden kiss, which is forbidden by consensus, "salam," so they say: "He greeted her," meaning he kissed her. The truth about which there is no doubt is keeping far from all temptations and doubts and their causes, and among the greatest of them is a man touching any part of a non-related woman's body. Blocking the means to what is forbidden is obligatory, as we have clarified in other places, and this is alluded to by the saying of the author of Maraqi al-Su'ud:

Blocking the means to what is forbidden is mandatory, just as opening them is to what is required.

Al-Shinqiti's commentary on the verse: His saying, ﴿Indeed, Allah has cursed the disbelievers and prepared for them a blaze﴾, up to His saying, ﴿a great curse﴾. The verses that clarify it have preceded many times.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 33, verse 72:

His statement, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, We offered the trust (amanah) to the heavens and the earth and the mountains, but they refused to bear it and were apprehensive of it, and man bore it. Indeed, he was ever wrongdoing and ignorant.﴾

In this noble verse, the Exalted mentions that He offered the trust (amanah), which is the obligations (al-taklif) together with what follows them of reward and punishment, to the heavens, the earth, and the mountains. They refused to bear it and were apprehensive of it, meaning they feared the consequences of bearing it, that there would arise for them the punishment and wrath of Allah. This offering, refusal, and apprehension are all true. Allah has created for the heavens, the earth, and the mountains a perception that only He, the Exalted, knows, and we do not know it. By that perception they comprehended the offering of the trust to them, and they refused and were apprehensive, meaning they feared.

Many verses and hadiths indicate the like of this. Among the verses indicating the perception of inanimate things is His statement, exalted is He, in Surat al-Baqarah, concerning stones: ﴿And indeed, among them are those that descend out of fear of Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah: 74]. He explicitly states that among stones there are those that descend out of the fear of Allah, and this fear which Allah attributes to some stones is by a perception that He, exalted is He, knows.

Among the verses indicating this is His statement, exalted is He: ﴿The seven heavens and the earth and whoever is in them exalt Him. And there is not a thing except that it exalts His praise, but you do not understand their exaltation﴾ [al-Isra': 44], up to the end of the verse. (p-259) Among them is His statement: ﴿And We subjected the mountains to exalt [Allah] along with David﴾ [al-Anbiya': 79], and other verses besides these.

Among the authentic hadiths indicating this is the story of the trunk of the date palm that moaned (hanin al-jidh), upon which the Prophet (ﷺ) used to deliver the sermon when he moved to the pulpit (minbar). It is in Sahih al-Bukhari and others.

Among them is what is established in Sahih Muslim from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "Indeed, I know a stone that used to greet me in Makkah." Similar examples are many. All of that mentioned in the Book and the Sunnah occurs by a perception that Allah knows and we do not know, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿But you do not understand their exaltation﴾ [al-Isra': 44]. Had the intended meaning of the exaltation of inanimate things been their indication of their Creator, we would understand it, as is known, and many verses have indicated that.

His statement, exalted is He, in this noble verse: ﴿And man bore it; indeed, he was ever wrongdoing and ignorant﴾. The apparent meaning is that by "man" is intended Adam, peace be upon him and our Prophet, and that the pronoun in His statement: ﴿Indeed, he was ever wrongdoing and ignorant﴾ refers to the word "man" itself, stripped of the intention of the one referred to, who is Adam.

The meaning is: that he, i.e., man who does not preserve the trust, ﴿was ever wrongdoing and ignorant﴾, meaning exceedingly wrongdoing and ignorant. The evidence for this is two matters:

The first: a Qur'anic indicator showing that man is divided in bearing the mentioned trust into one who is punished and one who is shown mercy, in His statement, exalted is He, immediately following it, connected to it: ﴿That Allah may punish the hypocrite men and hypocrite women and the polytheist men and polytheist women, and that Allah may accept repentance from the believing men and believing women. And ever is Allah Forgiving and Merciful﴾ [al-Ahzab: 73]. This indicates that the wrongdoing, ignorant one among mankind is the one punished, and Allah forbid, and they are the hypocrite men and hypocrite women, and the polytheist men and polytheist women, not the believing men and believing women. The lam in His statement "li-yu'adhdhiba" (that He may punish) is the lam of causation, and it is connected to His statement: ﴿And man bore it﴾.

The second matter: that the mentioned style, which is the return of the pronoun to the bare word without consideration of the detailed meaning, is known in the language in which the Qur'an was revealed, and it has come in fact in a verse of the Book of Allah, which is His statement, exalted is He: ﴿And no one is granted a long life or has a part of his life reduced except that it is in a Record﴾ [Fatir: 11]; because the pronoun in His statement "wa la yunqasu min 'umrihi" (nor is any of his life reduced) refers to the word "mu'ammar" (one granted long life) and not to its detailed meaning, as is evident. We have clarified this in Surat al-Furqan, in the discussion of His statement: ﴿And He placed therein a lamp and a moon giving light﴾ [al-Furqan: 61], and we explained there that this issue is the one known among the scholars of Arabic grammar as the issue of: "I have a dirham and its half", meaning half of another dirham, as you see.

Some of the people of knowledge who said that the pronoun in His statement: ﴿Indeed, he was ever wrongdoing and ignorant﴾ refers to Adam, said: the meaning is that he was wrongdoing toward himself and ignorant, meaning heedless of the consequences of matters and of the difficulties that follow the trust. The more apparent is what we have mentioned, and knowledge rests with Allah, the Exalted.
